content: Docker packages software and its dependencies into a portable container that runs on any machine with the Docker engine or Singularity (Apptainer). Most brainlife.io Apps run their software from a Docker container through Singularity. You can build a complete, standalone Docker container for your App. For brainlife.io, we recommend that you containerize only the App's environment and dependencies, and keep the main part of the App (the Python or MATLAB scripts that drive your algorithm) out of the container. Your scripts stay in your GitHub repository, and Singularity runs them inside the environment container at run time. For example: Here brainlife/dipy:0.13 is the environment container, and app.py comes from the App's repository and runs inside that environment. You can share one container across several Apps that you and your lab maintain. Always name a specific container version ("0.13" above), so that your App does not change when the container is updated. If you write a brainlife.app.json manifest, list the container image under runtime (see Describe your App with a manifest).

To build a Docker container, install Docker on your computer or use a server that has it. If you need help, contact the brainlife.io team. The steps below assume your App is already on GitHub and you are working in a clone of its repository on a machine with Docker.

Skip this section if you do not use MATLAB. MATLAB code needs a MATLAB license to run. If your App contains MATLAB code, compile it with the mcc command . The compiled program runs without a MATLAB license, against the MATLAB Runtime (MCR), which is free to distribute. You can write a script that compiles your MATLAB code. This example comes from an HPC cluster; adjust the module name and paths to your system. compile.sh The script writes a MATLAB script called build.m and runs it. build.m sets the MATLAB paths and runs mcc, which compiles your code into an executable that runs without a MATLAB license. The executable still needs the MATLAB Runtime (MCR) libraries, which you can download from MathWorks. The brainlife.io team maintains Docker images with the MATLAB Runtime, brainlife/mcr , that you can use to run compiled MATLAB code with Singularity. In build.m, add every MATLAB dependency of your code with addpath(). myapp is the name of the MATLAB entry function of your App; mcc writes an executable with the same name, myapp, into ./compiled. Some mcc options: -m ... names the main entry function of your App (the function that reads config.json and runs the whole App). -R -nodisplay sets the command-line options you would normally pass to MATLAB. -d ... sets where to write the executable. Avoid the root of the repository, to keep it tidy. If your App or its libraries read non-MATLAB files (MEX files, data files, models, templates, and so on), include them with -a. mcc adds

If your code loads custom data structures (for example with load('data.mat'), such as the sparse tensor array in encode's fe structure), addpath() is not enough to include their classes in the executable. Tell the compiler about them with a special comment like this: % function sptensor This tells the compiler to include the sptensor class.

There are many guides to writing a Dockerfile. A good place to start is Docker's Getting Started guide . Because most brainlife.io Apps run Docker containers through Singularity, a few details matter for your App to run correctly.

Singularity runs containers as a normal user, so some system setup has to happen when you build the image. When Docker installs system packages, it may not create the links for shared libraries until they are first used. Under Singularity the container runs as a normal user and cannot create them. Run ldconfig as the last command in your Dockerfile; it creates the links and cache for the shared libraries in the library directories:

Some older operating systems (such as RHEL 6) only let Singularity mount a host path if the same directory already exists in the container, because the kernel lacks overlay support. If your App must run on such a host, create the mount points in your Dockerfile. For example, for a cluster that mounts its storage under /N:

An App is a containerized program from a GitHub repository that takes datatypes in and produces datatypes out. On brainlife.io, any GitHub repository can become an App. The App catalog describes it this way: "Apps process data, taking in specific datatypes as input and producing resulting datatypes." An App usually does one short series of processing steps within a larger analysis. Write it so that other people can run it on their own data, not only to reproduce your results. Use well-known tools, keep the code readable and document what the App does. Every App: 1. Lives in a public repository on github.com. The code can be in MATLAB, Python, shell or any other language. 2. Has one executable file named main at the root of the repository. brainlife.io runs main on a compute resource, directly or through a batch scheduler such as Slurm (sbatch) or PBS (qsub). 3. Reads all its parameters from a config.json file. brainlife.io writes config.json into the working directory when a job starts. 4. Reads its input data from the paths listed in config.json. The file holds both the parameters (for example command-line options) and the paths to input files (for example t1.nii.gz). 5. Writes its output files into the working directory (./), in the structure defined by a datatype . See Datatypes. New Apps should also: 6. Before you write an App for brainlife.io, you should be comfortable with: 1. At least one programming language (MATLAB, Python, R, and so on). 2. The bash terminal and basic shell scripting. See Introduction to Bash . 3. git and GitHub , to publish your repository. 4. Basic concepts of high-performance computing (HPC). You can develop and test an App on your own computer, but brainlife.io runs most Apps on shared clusters. See: - Slurm on HPC clusters (Princeton Research Computing) 5. Containers. Apps run their software from a Docker container through Singularity. You do not need to build containers yourself (the brainlife.io team can help), but you should know what a container is and what Singularity does. See the Singularity introduction . Writing an App draws on programming, the Unix shell, git and HPC. The community list learn-neuroimaging/tutorials-and-resources collects online tutorials on these topics.

You normally follow these steps. 1. Make your algorithm run on your computer or local cluster with your test data. 2. Write a sample config.json. 3. Write main, which reads config.json and passes the values to your algorithm. See HelloWorld. 4. Publish the code as a public GitHub repository. 5. Add a brainlife.app.json manifest and a README based on the template, and check the manifest with python tools/blapp.py validate from the abcd-spec repository. 6. Register the App on brainlife.io (My Apps → App). This is where you define the parameters and input files that reach your App through config.json. See Registering an App. 7. Ask resource administrators to enable your App on their compute resources (below).

section: Enable an App on a compute resource
content: An App runs only on compute resources where it is enabled. Each user has access to a different set of resources, and brainlife.io provides shared public resources for everyone. If you want every brainlife.io user to be able to run your App, contact the brainlife.io team and ask for it to be enabled on the public resources. Discuss with the resource administrators how your App gets its dependencies and libraries. To keep this simple and reproducible, put your App's dependencies (not the App itself) in a Docker container and run your code inside that container with Singularity from your main. Most compute resources now provide Singularity (Apptainer), so containerized Apps can run on more resources.

section: What happens when someone runs your App
content: brainlife.io runs an App in these steps. 1. A user runs your App in a project, in a process or through a pipeline automation. 2. brainlife.io lists the compute resources that the user can use and that have your App enabled, and picks the best one (see Amaretti). 3. brainlife.io stages the input datasets from the project, or copies the working directory of an earlier job that produced them. 4. brainlife.io creates a working directory by cloning your repository (at the registered branch or tag), usually on the resource's scratch disk, and writes config.json with the user's parameters and the paths to the input files. 5. brainlife.io runs the start hook installed on the resource, as defined by the ABCD specification. In most cases you do not need to think about hooks. 6. On a batch cluster, the start hook submits your main to the local scheduler queue. 7. The scheduler runs main on a compute node. Your App runs your algorithm and writes its outputs into the working directory. 8. brainlife.io monitors the job and shows its status and logs to the user. 9. When the job finishes, the outputs are archived as datasets in the project (if the user chose to archive them).

Apps exchange data through datatypes. A datatype is a file and directory structure, defined by developers, that holds a specific kind of data. Datatypes keep Apps interoperable. Some examples of registered datatypes: neuro/anat/t1w (t1.nii.gz) neuro/anat/t2w (t2.nii.gz) neuro/dwi (diffusion data with bvecs and bvals) neuro/freesurfer (the whole FreeSurfer output) neuro/track/tck (track.tck with streamlines) neuro/dtiinit (dtiInit output directory) generic/images (a list of images) raw (unstructured data, often used during development) Your App should read one or more of these datatypes and write its output in the format of another datatype. When you use existing datatypes, your App can read data produced by other Apps, and other Apps can use your outputs as their inputs. To propose a new datatype, ask in the #datatype channel on the brainlife.io Slack. See Datatypes for more detail. - A Quarter Century of Unix by Doug McIlroy Follow the Do One Thing and Do It Well principle: split a complex workflow into several smaller Apps (but no more than is practical). Smaller Apps are easier to reuse, run in parallel and can each run on the most suitable compute resource. Before you write an App, browse the Apps and Datatypes catalogs to check that the App you need does not already exist. If a similar App exists, contact its developer and discuss whether the feature you need can be added.

Every App should have a clear upper bound on the compute resources and time it needs. Most main scripts start with batch scheduler directives like these: These lines tell the batch scheduler how much time and how many resources your App needs. If your job exceeds them, the scheduler stops it. On an HPC system, the scheduler reserves the requested time and resources and charges service units (SUs) for them. Keep the request as low as you can: measure how much CPU and memory your App usually uses and set the directives to match. If your App runs for a long time, set the walltime high enough. Larger requests cost more and also wait longer in the queue for the resources to become free. Be conservative with cpus-per-task (or ppn). Most schedulers charge the number of CPUs you request times the run time. For example, a 2-hour job with 16 cores costs 2 x 16 = 32 units. If your job only uses 4 cores, request 4, and it costs 2 x 4 = 8 units. People use brainlife.io to process their own data, not only to reproduce the developer's results. Your App should handle a wide range of input data, not just the data you used to develop it. This is hard, and Apps usually take time to become robust. Users may submit data that is much larger or more complex than you expected, and sometimes the job cannot finish within the time limit. To handle this, make your App able to restart and resume from where it stopped. For example, if your App runs 3 steps that each take an hour, make each step check whet

Your App can write a file named product.json into its working directory to send information back to brainlife.io. It is the counterpart of config.json: config.json passes parameters from the user to the App, and product.json passes information from the App back to brainlife.io when the job finishes. Use it to tell the user something about the run, or to store small results that you can later collect across many subjects quickly. Keep product.json to a few kilobytes. Use product.json to: 1. Show messages, graphs (Plotly) and images on brainlife.io. 2. Store a small amount of data that you can later collect across many output datasets. 3. Set annotations (dataset tags), metadata or datatype tags on the output datasets. Each use is explained below.

Once your App is in a public GitHub repository, register it on brainlife.io so that you and other people can find it and run it. Registering takes two steps: create the App, then fill in its settings (configuration parameters, inputs and outputs). Before you register, add a brainlife.app.json manifest and a README to the repository (see Describe your App with a manifest).

1. In the sidebar, select My Apps. 2. Select App (the button with a plus sign). The Create app dialog opens: "Register a processing app from a GitHub repository. Apps accept specific datatypes as input and produce resulting datatypes." 3. Enter a Name (for example "Freesurfer recon-all"). 4. Enter the GitHub repository as orgname/reponame (for example yourname/app-name), not the full GitHub URL. 5. Choose the Branch or tag to run. If you choose master or main, the dialog warns "Avoid releasing an app from master or main." Register a version branch or tag instead (see Versioning tips). 6. Select Create app. brainlife.io creates the App and opens its settings. To change the settings later, open the App page and select Edit. The settings have four tabs: Details, Configurations (n), Inputs (n) and Outputs (n). Select Save Changes when you are done.

The Details tab has four sections. Details ("Name, description, and avatar shown for this app.") Name: the App name shown in the catalog. Description override: leave it empty to use the GitHub repository description (see README, description and topics). Avatar: the URL of an image for your App. Use a square image with an https:// URL. Many Apps are registered, and the avatar helps people recognize yours. Access ("Who can edit this app, and which projects can use it.") Maintainers: the people who can edit this App. Projects: by default an App is public, so anyone can find and run it. To make it available only to some projects ("Restrict access to selected projects"), add those projects here. Only members of those projects can then use the App. This is useful while you are still developing the App, or if it only works on data from one project. Source code ("GitHub repository and branch or tag for this app.") Repository and Github Branch or Tag: the repository and the branch or tag that brainlife.io runs. brainlife.io records the branch used for each job, so people can reproduce an output with the same version of your code. If you register master or main and keep changing it, people cannot reproduce results exactly. When the App is ready, create a release branch (for example 1.0) and register that. See Versioning tips. Deprecated ("Point users to a replacement, hide this app from listings, or delete it.") Replacement app: the App that replaces this one. Mark as removed: hide the

The Inputs tab ("Input datasets, datatypes, file mappings, and optional filters.") lists the input data your App expects. Select Add Input to add one. For each input, set: ID: an identifier for the input (it is not the key used in config.json). Your App can use this ID to find information about the input at run time in config.json (under ._inputs). Datatype: the datatype of the input. Description: how your App uses this input. Datatype tags: tags that the input datasets must have. "Prefix tags with ! to exclude datasets with those tags." Users can only select datasets that match. See Datatypes. If you do not know which datatype to use, ask in the #datatype channel on the brainlife.io Slack.

After you choose the datatype, decide how each of its files appears in config.json. A datatype is made of files and directories. Under File mapping, enter a config.json key for each file or directory your App uses. Use Add optional file mapping to map more of the datatype's files. For example, the neuro/dwi datatype has the files dwi, bvecs and bvals. If your App only uses the dwi file and you want its path under the key dwi, map it like this: When someone runs your App, brainlife.io writes a config.json like this: Your App reads config.json and uses the value of dwi as the path to the input image. To use all 3 files of neuro/dwi, create 3 file mappings: dwi, bvecs and bvals. Object subsetting (experimental): if your App only uses part of an input, list the file paths it needs, one per line (* matches any characters; paths are relative to the root of the datatype). Leave it blank to transfer the whole input. Listing only what you need reduces scratch disk use and transfer time.

Optional: "User can submit this App without this input specified". Leave it unchecked for a required input. If the input is optional and the user does not provide it, config.json has none of the keys from its file mapping. Multi: "Allow user to select multiple datasets in an array". The selected datasets are placed in a JSON array, even if the user selects only one. For example, the config.json above becomes: If an input has more than one file mapping, the order of the datasets in each array is the same across all mappings.

The Outputs tab ("Output directories, datatypes, tags, and archive settings.") lists the datasets your App produces. Select Add Output to add one. You choose the datatype (discuss new datatypes in the #datatype Slack channel), and your App must write the files with the names and structure that the datatype defines. For each output, set: Output Directory: the directory, inside the working directory, where your App writes this output. In the example above, the App writes a directory called mask with the file mask.nii.gz inside it. Datatype: the datatype of the output. Description: "Describe what this output is, and what the user can do with it". Write as much as is useful. Datatype tags: tags that describe the output more precisely. For example, the screenshot shows an App that outputs anat/t1w with the tag acpcaligned. An App that only works with ACPC-aligned anat/t1w can require the same tag on its input. * Datatype tags/metadata passthrough: "Take all datatype tags and metadata associated with the specified app input, and apply it to this output". Some Apps work as a *filter*: they take a dataset and produce another of the same datatype, and should *add* tags rather than replace them. Choose the input to copy tags and metadata from. For example, if the input has the tag defaced, the output has both acpcaligned and defaced. * Archive this output by default: "Uncheck this if this output is rarely used to reduce the size of archive."

Your App may produce output that no other App is meant to use, at least at first. Use the raw datatype to output and archive such data. Avoid raw as an input datatype: if you need another App's raw output as your input, the other developer and you should define a new datatype so that both Apps can work together through it. Ask in the #datatype channel on brainlife.slack.com to register a new datatype, or to find other developers interested in it.

The Configurations tab ("Configuration parameters shown when users run this app.") lists the parameters users can set. Select Add String, Add Number, Add Boolean or Add Enum to add one. An enum lets users choose from a list of options (Add option; each option has a Label, Description and Value). For each parameter, set: config.json key: the key under which the value appears in config.json. Description: shown next to the parameter. Give enough detail for both new and experienced users. Placeholder (string and number): text shown inside the field when it is empty, for example the expected format or a sample value. Min and Max (number): the allowed range. Default value. Options: "This is an optional Input", "This is an advanced option" (shown under the advanced configuration section), "This is read-only" (fixed to the default value), and for strings "This is a multi-line input". For new users brainlife.io is for both new and experienced users. For new users, describe each parameter and how to choose a good value (link to a web page or to your README). Make as many parameters optional as you can, and detect good values at run time when the user does not set them. For experienced users Your App should not be a black box for experienced users. Let them set or override any parameter, so they stay in control of how the algorithm works. Select Save Changes, then open the App page and check that everything looks right.

brainlife.io reuses information from your GitHub repository. Description and topics The GitHub repository description is shown as the App description (unless you set Description override). Write a description that says what the App does and what users can do with its output. GitHub topics are shown as the App's Tags and help people find your App. Reuse topics that other Apps already use. Avoid using many topics, and avoid topics that no other App uses. README.md The App page shows the README of your repository under About. You can include images, LaTeX equations and any standard Markdown . Start from the brainlife App README template , which follows the layout of the FreeSurfer App : badges, an "At a glance" block, versions, how to run the App, outputs, troubleshooting, citations, authors, funding and license. The "At a glance" block is generated from your manifest (see below). Include: What your App does and how (tools and libraries used). What your App produces and what users can do with it. Diagrams or sample output images. How the algorithm works. The compute it needs (how long it runs, minimum memory and CPU cores). How others can contribute (do you accept pull requests?). * Papers to cite and a list of contributors. brainlife.io is for both new and experienced neuroscience researchers. Write for both.

section: Describe your App with a manifest
content: New Apps should add a brainlife.app.json file at the root of each App branch. The manifest describes what the App does, so that people and AI agents can find an App, connect its inputs, set its parameters and predict what a run needs without reading its scripts. It is defined in ABCD specification version 2 (draft) . The manifest only describes your App. Adding it does not change how your App runs, and brainlife.io does not read it yet: the App page and config.json still come from the settings you enter on brainlife.io. Keep the two consistent. The manifest must validate against schema/brainlife-app-2.0.schema.json . Its main fields: | Field | What it holds | |---|---| | summary | One sentence (up to 350 characters): the GitHub description and the brainlife.io tagline | | description | What the App does, when to use it and when not to | | inputs[], outputs[] | Datatype by name (for example neuro/anat/t1w), datatype tags, a description, and for inputs the config.json keys that receive the files | | parameters[] | Typed (string, integer, number, boolean, enum), with description, default, units, range and options | | runtime | Container image, suggested resources and required licences | | software, citations, failure_modes, topics, doi | Tools and versions, papers to cite, known errors and their fixes, search topics, the App DOI | A complete example is examples/freesurfer-7.3.2.brainlife.app.json . section: Enable the App on compute resources
content: After you register your App, it must be enabled on the compute resources where it will run. A resource can be a VM, an HPC cluster or a public or private cloud. Only the administrators of a resource can enable Apps on it: on the resource page they keep the list of enabled Apps ("Only apps listed here are submitted to this resource."). Contact the administrator of each resource where you want your App to run. If you do not know who administers a resource, contact the brainlife.io team. If you have your own compute resources, you can register them under My Resources and enable your App there to test it. See Registering a resource. On a private resource, only you (and the projects you share it with) can run the Apps enabled there. For everyone to be able to run your App, it must be enabled on the brainlife.io public resources. Once your App is enabled, the resources appear under Computing Resources on the App page. Most Apps run their software inside a container. The next step is to containerize your App, as explained in Containerizing an App.
Submodules let several GitHub repositories share code. If you maintain several similar Apps, they are a good way to keep the common code in one place.

Run a command like this at the root of your repository: Do not use an SSH URL for a submodule (like git@github.com:something/something.git). brainlife.io cannot clone your App if a submodule uses a git@ URL. Check and fix the URLs in the .gitmodules file.
brainlife.io does not require a particular git branching scheme, and you can follow your group's own practice. These are the guidelines we suggest.

Develop on the repository's default branch (main or master). Pull from the remote often to reduce merge conflicts. Use local branches for each feature, but do not push them. When a feature or fix is tested on your local branch, merge it into your local default branch and push it.

You can test an App on your computer by running main, or on an HPC system with the start script if the ABCD default hooks are on your PATH. Do not commit and push changes to GitHub just to test them on brainlife.io.

section: Create a branch for each release
content: When all changes are made and tested, create a release branch from the default branch. You can create one in the GitHub web interface. Then point your App on brainlife.io to the new branch: open the App, select Edit, and on the Details tab set Github Branch or Tag under Source code. When you register a new App, the Create app dialog warns "Avoid releasing an app from master or main." You can use tags instead of branches, but a tag cannot take a quick bug fix later. A tag only points to one commit, which a commit ID also does. We recommend a branch for each release.

If you find a critical bug after you create a release branch, fix it on the default branch first and test it (on your computer and on brainlife.io). Then apply the same fix to every affected release branch, for example with cherry-pick , since you probably do not want to merge every other change made since the branch was created. Change release branches only for critical bug fixes, so that your App stays reproducible. If your repository has a brainlife.app.json manifest, keep the copy on each release branch up to date. Its version field is the name of that branch.

If you do not know semantic versioning, read semver.org . Name branches with the major and minor version (like "2.3"), without the patch number: the patch number goes up with each bug fix, and you do not need a new branch for each fix. If you make changes that are not backward compatible, consider registering a new App with a new major version, so that people can still run the previous version.

To find Apps that take a given datatype as input (for example neuro/anat/t1w): Each result looks like this: Read the Type: line as (inputs) -> (outputs), each written as : : Input: an input with ID 0 of datatype neuro/anat/t1w. Output: an output with ID 0 of datatype neuro/anat/t1w with the datatype tag acpc_aligned. A [] after a datatype means the input accepts several datasets; a ? means it is optional. Use --output-datatype to find Apps that produce a datatype. You can repeat both options.
Search App names and descriptions: Other options: --id , --doi , --skip, --limit and --json. ---

To run an App, give: 1. --id : the App to run. 2. --project : the project where the outputs are archived. 3. --input : : one for each input, using the input IDs from the Type: line. --preferred-resource : a compute resource you would like the job to run on (find IDs with bl resource query). brainlife.io uses it if it can. --branch : run another branch of the App's repository. section: 3. Wait for a job (`bl app wait`)
content: When you run an App, brainlife.io creates a job (a task in Amaretti). To wait until it finishes and its outputs are archived: In a terminal, the CLI prints the job status as it changes, then (done waiting). ---
This bash script uploads a T1-weighted image, runs ACPC alignment on it, waits for the job and downloads the outputs: ```bash #!/usr/bin/env bash set -e
bl login --ttl 30 PROJECT_ID=" " SUBJECT="sub-001"

echo "Uploading T1w image..." UPLOADRES=$(bl data upload \ --project "$PROJECTID" \ --datatype neuro/anat/t1w \ --subject "$SUBJECT" \ --t1 ./rawdata/sub-001T1w.nii.gz \ --tag "raw" \ --json) INPUTT1ID=$(echo "$UPLOADRES" | jq -r '.id') echo "T1w uploaded with ID: $INPUTT1ID"

echo "Running ACPC alignment..." APPID="5a0def2eb2f8e6004a894f3b" APPTASK=$(bl app run \ --id "$APPID" \ --project "$PROJECTID" \ --input "0:$INPUTT1ID" \ --config ' ' \ --tag "acpccli" \ --json) TASKID=$(echo "$APPTASK" | jq -r '.id') echo "Job created: $TASK_ID"
echo "Waiting for the job..." bl app wait --id "$TASK_ID"

echo "Querying output datasets..." OUTPUTIDS=$(bl data query --taskid "$TASKID" --json | jq -r '.[].id') for OUTID in $OUTPUTIDS; do echo "Downloading output dataset: $OUTID" bl data download --id "$OUTID" --directory "./outputs/$SUBJECT/$OUTID" done echo "Done." ```

Brain data across scales. One place to analyze, share and publish it. brainlife.io is an open platform from The University of Texas at Austin for brain data across scales: electron and light microscopy, PS-OCT, MRI, fMRI, EEG and MEG. You bring data in from your computer or from public archives, run reproducible analyses as Apps on shared supercomputers, look at the results in your browser, and publish them with a DOI. brainlife.io is free for researchers. This page introduces the main ideas in the order you meet them. Each section links to a page with the details. When you are ready, go to Getting started. If you have questions, see Contact for email and the brainlife.io Slack.

A project is your workspace. It holds your data, your processing, your notebooks and your publications, and you share it with your team. Each person in a project is an admin, a member or a guest: admins edit the settings, members process data, and guests view. A project is public or private. To find your projects, select My Projects in the sidebar. To browse projects that others share, select Public Projects. See Projects.

A dataset is one item of project data: the files of one datatype for one subject (and session), for example the T1-weighted image of subject 01. You add datasets to a project in three ways: - Copy them from Public Datasets, which brings together DANDI, EMBER, BossDB, OpenNeuro and the brainlife.io Dataset Library. See Public Datasets. - Copy them from another project. - Upload your own data. See Project data for the upload routes that work today.

A datatype describes which files a dataset contains, so that Apps can exchange data. An App declares the datatypes it takes in and the datatypes it produces, so the output of one App can be the input of the next. Browse them under Datatypes in the sidebar. See Datatypes.

An App is a containerized program, built from a GitHub repository, that takes datatypes in and produces datatypes out. Any GitHub repository can become an App. Commonly used tools such as FreeSurfer, FSL, MRtrix3, DIPY, fMRIPrep, QSIPrep and ANTs run as Apps, along with hundreds of others in the Apps catalog. You run Apps in a project in two ways: - Processes: choose data and Apps by hand, one step at a time. See Processes. - Pipeline: add automations that run an App for every subject and session that has the inputs. See Pipelines. To write your own App, see Developing Apps.

A resource is a computer, a cluster or a cloud, that runs your jobs. Public resources are shared by everyone; you can also register private resources and enable them for your projects. Jobs run on TACC, Jetstream2 and ACCESS. See Public Resources and My Resources in the sidebar, and Registering a resource.

You look at data in your browser, without downloading it. Select a dataset and choose a viewer for its datatype, for example NiiVue for volumes, surfaces and streamlines, or Neuroglancer for large microscopy and EM volumes. Some datatypes also offer desktop programs streamed to your browser. See Datatypes.

When your results are ready, you publish them. A publication is a citable record with a DOI that describes and shares your results; the DOI is assigned when you create it. A publication can hold releases of your data and the Apps and notebooks that produced them. Find yours under My Publications and everyone's under Public Publications. See Publications.
Each project can launch Jupyter notebooks against its data, from a blank template or from a notebook published with a publication. See Analysis with notebooks. Ready to start? Get started here.

brainlife.io lets you make a compute resource, such as a cloud system or a high-performance computing cluster, available to specific users and projects. By default, shared public resources are available to all users, and most brainlife.io Apps are enabled on them. Because everyone uses the public resources, jobs sometimes wait in the queue. You can register your own compute resource in these cases: 1. You have access to your own HPC resource, and you'd like to use it to run brainlife.io Apps, for better performance, or better access control. 2. You are an app developer and you'd like to use your own resource to troubleshoot your apps on your own resource, for easier debugging. 3. You are an app developer and your app can only run on specialized resources (like Hadoop, Spark, etc..) that the public brainlife.io resources do not provide. Only brainlife.io administrators can make a resource available to all projects. To share your resource that way, contact the brainlife.io administrators. Resource owner decides which apps are allowed to run on their resource. If you register a resource and enable apps on it, only you can run those apps on that resource. If you are publishing your app, and you want all users to be able to execute your app, contact the brainlife.io administrators to enable your App on the public resources. Although we do our best to limit access to your dataset on shared resources, we recommend registering your own resource for added security especially if you ar
Before you can register your resource, you should make sure that your resource is ready to run brainlife Apps.

ABCD Hooks are used to start, stop and monitor apps on remote resources. Some app provides its own hooks, but many of them relies on default hooks that are installed on each resource. As a resource provider, you need to provide these default hooks and make them available by setting $PATH. If you are not sure how to write these scripts, you can install and use the default brainlife.io ABCD hooks: Then, add one of following to your ~/.bashrc For PBS cluster For Slurm cluster (for most HPC systems) For direct execution - no batch submission manager (like.. In order to process data, you will need scratch / workdir to host your input/output files as well as any temporary files generated. Most HPC systems provide a scratch storage system; on some systems you need to request a scratch allocation first and configure your brainlife resource to use it. You can then create a directory inside your scratch directory such as brainlife keeps data on scartch volume up to 3 months. Most likely, you will not be able to keep your data that long without running out of your storage space. Please purge unnsed data periodically and monitor your storage usage (use quota command). You can run a command like this to search and purge unused workdirs (create a script and run this, or setup a cron job to run it automatically)

brainlife.io expects these binaries on every resource. Please make sure following commands are installed. jq (command line JSON parser that many brainlife.io Apps use to read config.json) git (used to clone / update apps installed) singularity (user level container execution engine) node (some app uses node to generate job submission file) For singularity, you can either install it on the system (apt install singularity-container with neurodebian, or yum install epel-release singularity for yum based systems), or for most HPC systems you can simply add module load singularity in your ~/.modules file. By default, singularity uses user's home directory to cache docker images (and /tmp to create a merged container image to run). If you have limited amount of home directory space, you will need to override it by setting SINGULARITY_CACHEDIR. * Please replace with your username, and make sure specified directories exists. singularity by default does not expose any mounted file systems inside the container. To register your resource: 1. In the sidebar, select My Resources. 2. Select Resource (the plus button). 3. You should not share the same directory with other resources. Amaretti is brainlife.io's workflow service. Its README describes it as "a light-weight, cross-resource, multi-user task orchestration service written in Node.js". It is a meta-scheduler: it does not replace the batch schedulers of compute clusters, but works on top of them (Slurm, PBS and others, and plain VMs), and can also submit to AWS Batch. Amaretti takes care of the work that running jobs on many resources involves: choosing a compute resource, staging input data, starting and monitoring jobs, copying working directories between resources, and cleaning up scratch space. In brainlife.io, each run of an App is a job. In Amaretti a job is a task, and related tasks are grouped in an instance (a process in the web app). ---

Amaretti connects to compute resources over SSH, keeps tasks, instances and resources in MongoDB, uses Redis as a cache, and publishes status changes on a RabbitMQ (AMQP) message bus, which the event service passes on to the web app and the CLI. ---

When a task is submitted, Amaretti scores every resource the user can use and picks the one with the highest score: 1. App enabled: a resource only runs Apps that its administrators enabled on it, each with a score. A resource without the App, with a score of 0, with no free capacity (each resource sets the maximum number of tasks it runs at once) or whose status is not OK is not used. 2. Bonuses: the score goes up by 5 if the task's dependencies ran on that resource (no data needs to move), by 10 if it is a private resource of the user, and by 15 if the user prefers it (for example --preferred-resource in the CLI). The App page shows these resources under Computing Resources, and GET /resource/best returns the result of this selection (see the REST API). If no resource can run the task yet, it stays requested until one can. ---

A task moves through these states: requested: the task is registered and waits for its dependencies and for a resource. running: the inputs are staged in the task's working directory on the resource and the job has been submitted to the resource (for example with the start hook, which submits main to the scheduler). finished: the job completed successfully. Outputs the user chose to archive are then archived as datasets. failed: the job failed, for example with a non-zero exit code, or the scheduler stopped it (time limit, memory). A task also fails if a task it depends on failed ("Dependency failed.") or was removed ("Dependency removed."). stop_requested and stopped: a user asked to stop the task, and it was stopped. removed: the working directory was deleted from the resource. ---

If a task needs the output of a task that ran on another resource, Amaretti copies the parent task's working directory directly from one resource to the other, without passing the data through the brainlife.io servers: 1. Amaretti starts an ssh-agent holding the key for the source resource. 2. It connects to the destination resource over SSH with agent forwarding. 3. On the destination resource it runs rsync to pull the parent task's directory from the source resource. 4. When the copy ends, the agent is stopped. ---

Tasks can depend on other tasks: - A task does not start until all the tasks it depends on are finished ("Waiting on dependencies"). - If a dependency fails or is removed, the task fails. - Tasks in the same instance share a working area on the resource, so a task can read its parents' outputs there without a transfer when they ran on the same resource. ---

Working directories live on the scratch disks of compute resources and are temporary: 1. A task can set a removedate. After that date, housekeeping deletes its working directory. 2. Without a removedate, a task's working directory is deleted when the task is more than 90 days old. 3. When the working directory is gone, the task becomes removed. 4. Outputs that were archived as datasets in a project (2. Data) are stored by brainlife.io and do not depend on the working directory. Archive any output you want to keep. ---

Opening a new SSH connection for every command is slow and can trip the connection limits of institutional firewalls. Amaretti keeps SSH connections to resources open and reuses them for commands, file transfers and log reads. ---

Amaretti runs Apps that follow the ABCD (Application for Big Computational Data) specification : - From GitHub: an App is a GitHub repository. Each task records the branch it ran (service_branch), so results can be reproduced. - Hooks: Amaretti starts, monitors and stops a task with the start, status and stop hooks installed on the resource (or provided by the App; see Custom hooks). The default start hook runs the App's main. - Working directory: Amaretti clones the App into the task's working directory and writes config.json there, with the user's parameters and the paths to the input data. The App writes its outputs into the same directory, in the structure of the output datatypes. - Containers: most Apps run their software from a Docker container with Singularity (Apptainer) on HPC clusters, or Docker on cloud resources. ---

brainlife.io is built from a set of microservices . The two main ones are the Warehouse, which manages projects, data, Apps and publications, and Amaretti, brainlife.io's workflow service, which runs jobs on compute resources. The services talk to each other through REST APIs and an AMQP message bus. All web traffic reaches them through an nginx proxy. Monitoring and operations services are not shown in the diagram. Jobs run on shared compute resources (TACC, Jetstream2 and ACCESS) and on resources that users register themselves.

Amaretti orchestrates the jobs (tasks) that run Apps across compute resources. It works on top of each resource's own batch scheduler (such as Slurm or PBS): it picks a resource for each job, stages the inputs, starts and monitors the job, copies working directories between resources with rsync, and cleans up scratch space. See Amaretti and the Amaretti REST API.
The authentication service stores user accounts, handles sign-up and sign-in, and issues JWT tokens that the other services check without a session (stateless authentication ).

The event service lets the web app and the CLI subscribe to an event stream over a WebSocket. Services publish events such as job (task) status changes and dataset updates. Other services subscribe to these events with a valid token to receive them in real time, or queue them for event handlers.

The Warehouse provides most of brainlife.io's features. The web app and the CLI call the Warehouse API for most requests. The Warehouse organizes datasets in projects, runs pipeline automations, asks Amaretti to run jobs and to move data between compute resources, and stages and archives datasets. The web app is written in React . Modular processing App developers can register datatypes. Apps exchange data through datatypes, which keeps them modular: each App does one kind of processing (alignment, tracking, statistics, and so on), more code is reused, and developers can focus on what is new in their App. For example, a statistician writing a statistical method does not need to handle preprocessing, and a developer writing a tractography App does not need to write the analysis of the streamlines, which tract profile Apps already do. For users, modular Apps make it easier to build a workflow from interchangeable parts and to try a newer version or a different algorithm for one step. Combining Apps freely also makes incompatibilities more likely. For example, an App may take anat/t1w input but only work well on ACPC-aligned images. To reduce this risk, datasets carry datatype tags. An App can require certain datatype tags on its inputs, so users cannot run it on incompatible datasets. Apps process one subject at a time. To run an App on many subjects, brainlife.io submits one job per subject. Amaretti can then send each job to an HPC or high-throughput system, and to several re

The brainlife.io CLI is mostly used to upload and download data between brainlife.io and your computer. It can also run Apps, wait for jobs and query projects, datatypes, resources, publications and Apps. It is written in Node.js and distributed through npm. Unlike the web app, you install it yourself and keep it up to date. See Installing the CLI.

You can look at datasets in your browser: every output opens in NiiVue or Neuroglancer. NiiVue shows volumes, surfaces and streamlines, and Neuroglancer shows large electron and light microscopy volumes. These viewers run in your browser and load the data through the brainlife.io API. Some datatypes can also open in familiar desktop tools, such as FSLeyes or mrview, run in a container on a brainlife.io server and streamed to your browser (abcd-novnc ). You only need a web browser; you do not install the tools or download the data. See Visualizing datatypes and datasets.

This page is for researchers and developers who want to contribute to ezBIDS , the web tool that converts DICOM (and MEG) data to BIDS in the browser. ezBIDS reads the uploaded data, finds the information BIDS needs, and writes it to a file that the ezBIDS web interface reads and displays. This file is ezBIDScore.json. To add support for something new (for example a new MRI or PET sequence), you need to understand what ezBIDScore.json contains so that you can produce the same structure for the web interface. To use ezBIDS, see the ezBIDS user guide.

ezBIDS covers neuroscience data: neurophysiology, neuroimaging and microscopy. The web app converts MRI, PET and MEG through ezBIDS_core.json (below). EEG, iEEG, NIRS, EMG and microscopy are handled by aimport, a local engine in the same repository (aimport/) that reuses ezBIDS's mapping, conversion and defacing, adds an AI agent and a plan a person approves, de-identifies on the user's computer and validates against BIDS v1.11.2. It is driven by bl aimport (the brainlife.io Python CLI, pybrainlife, branch enh/cli) or, in the future, ezBIDS desktop. aimport is not released yet. User guide: aimport; engine API and internals: aimport/README.md.

When a user starts uploading data, ezBIDS creates a new session with the (post)/session API. A session holds one ezBIDS upload and conversion. For each session, ezBIDS creates a record in the session collection of the database (its MongoDB ID is the session ID) and a working directory named after the session ID on the backend server, where all uploaded data is stored. When all files are uploaded, the client calls (patch)/session/uploaded/:session_id, which sets the session state to "uploaded" so that the ezBIDS handler knows the session is ready for preprocessing.

The backend server polls for uploaded sessions. When it finds one, it sets the session state to "preprocessing" and runs the preprocessing script. The script uncompresses all compressed folders and files, runs dcm2niix, and writes a list of all the NIfTI and JSON sidecar files. ezBIDS_core.py analyzes these files and writes ezBIDS_core.json. When preprocessing is complete, the session state is set to "analyzed". The preprocessing step then loads ezBIDS_core.json and copies its contents to the ezBIDS collection of the database (not the session collection) under the original key.

section: 3. The user works with the session in the web interface
content: The web interface polls the session state, sees that preprocessing is complete, and loads ezBIDS_core.json with the (get)/download/:sessionid/ezBIDScore.json API. The user then reviews and corrects its contents.

Before finalizing, the user can deface the anatomical images. The web interface then calls (post)/session/:session_id/deface with the list of images to deface. The backend stores the list as deface.json in the working directory (workdir) and sets the session state to "deface". The defacing handler finds sessions in the "deface" state, sets them to "defacing" and runs the deface.sh script. When defacing is complete, it sets the session state to "defaced". deface.sh creates these files in the workdir: 1. deface.finished (the anatomical files that were defaced) 2. deface.failed (the anatomical files that could not be defaced) The web interface polls these files to see which images were defaced. The user then chooses whether to use each defaced image: each object has a field defaceSelection set to "original" or "defaced".

When the user selects Finalize, the web interface calls (post)/session/:session_id/finalize with this content from memory ($root): The API stores this as finalized.json in the workdir and copies it to the ezBIDS collection under the updated key (next to original). The session state becomes "finalized". This starts the finalize handler on the server, which sets the state to "bidsing" and runs bids.sh to build the BIDS structure from the information in each object. When it is done, the session state is set to "finished".
When the session state is "finished", the user can download the BIDS folder with the download API, or send it to other services (such as a brainlife.io project or OpenNeuro).

This tutorial shows you how to automate processing on brainlife.io. In earlier tutorials you added datasets to a process and ran Apps one at a time. That works well for testing on one subject, but large cohorts (dozens, hundreds or thousands of subjects) need automation. A project's pipeline is its set of automations. An automation runs an App for every subject (and session) that has the inputs and does not yet have the output. When an upstream automation archives its outputs, the next automation finds them and runs. In this tutorial you build an anatomical T1w pipeline that chains: 1. FSL Anat (T1w): brain extraction, bias correction and ACPC alignment. 2. FreeSurfer 7.3.2: cortical surface reconstruction and subcortical parcellation. 3. Multi-Atlas Transfer Tool (MaTT): maps the Glasser HCP-MMP cortical atlas. > [!NOTE] Prerequisites > Before you build a pipeline, make sure you know how to navigate a project and run an App by hand, as described in the Introduction to brainlife.io tutorial. ---

section: How Automations Work: Datatypes, Datatype Tags and Annotations
content: Automations react to the datasets in your project: - Input matching: each automation looks in your project for datasets of a given datatype (for example anat/t1w). Filters on datatype tags and Annotations (for example acpc_aligned) pick the right dataset when a subject has more than one match. - Running: when a subject has a matching input and lacks the output, the automation creates a process and runs the App with the settings you chose. - Output annotations and chaining: the automation archives its outputs with the Annotations you set (for example preprocessed, freesurfer). A downstream automation that filters on those annotations finds the new outputs and runs. ---

1. Create a new private project, or open your existing tutorial project. 2. Open the Sample Dataset. 3. Open its data list. 4. Filter by datatype anat/t1w. > [!WARNING] Select Only T1w Data > For this tutorial, select only anat/t1w datasets. Do not select DWI or fMRI datasets. 5. Select the checkboxes next to 2–3 subjects, select Copy to project, choose your tutorial project, and confirm. ---

section: Step 2: Add Automations to the Pipeline
content: Open your tutorial project and go to 3. Processing → Pipeline. Each automation is added in four steps: Select App, Configure App Settings, Configure Inputs and Configure Outputs. Select Next to move between steps and Complete to save.

1. Select + Automation. 2. Select App: search for FSL Anat (T1) (5e3c87ae9362b7166cf9c7f4) and select it. 3. Configure App Settings: - Turn on crop, reorient and bias. - Set the template to MNI1521MM. 4. Configure Inputs: leave the filters empty so the automation uses any raw anat/t1w dataset. 5. Configure Outputs: - Tick "Archive this output". - Under Annotations, add preprocessed and acpcaligned. These annotations let later automations tell aligned T1w scans from raw scans. 6. Select Complete. ---

1. Select + Automation. 2. Select App: search for Freesurfer 7.3.2 (5fe1056057aacd480f2f8e48). 3. Configure App Settings: turn on hippocampal and thalamicnuclei segmentation. 4. Configure Inputs: filter the T1w input on the annotations acpc_aligned and preprocessed. FreeSurfer then runs only on the output of automation 1, never on the unaligned raw image. 5. Configure Outputs: tick "Archive this output" and add the annotation freesurfer. 6. Select Complete. ---

1. Select + Automation. 2. Select App: search for Multi-Atlas Transfer Tool (MaTT) (6016dcdc321a4aafce6decd5). 3. Configure App Settings: select hcp-mmp-b (the Glasser 180-node atlas) as the atlas. 4. Configure Inputs: FreeSurfer produces its own datatype (freesurfer), so MaTT finds the FreeSurfer outputs without extra filters. 5. Configure Outputs: tick "Archive this output" and add the annotation Glasser. 6. Select Complete. ---

section: Step 3: Activate and Monitor the Pipeline
content: 1. Make sure each automation is set to Active. Open an automation (View details) to see and change its switch. 2. Go to 3. Processing → Summary or Processes. 3. The automations find your T1w subjects, create processes and send the jobs to available compute resources. 4. Select a process to see its status and logs. On Summary, resolve anything listed under Needs Action (for example an ambiguous input). ---

1. Automation: once your automations are set up, every new subject you add to the project runs through the whole pipeline without manual steps. 2. Quality control: use annotations as checkpoints (for example, run tractography only on datasets annotated as passing QA). 3. Reproducibility: every output records its provenance, and you can publish your data and the Apps you used with a citable DOI.

pageTitle: Using brainlife.io with Amazon Web Services
content: OME-Zarr is a format for storing bioimaging data, often used in microscopy workflows. If you’re storing an OME-Zarr dataset in S3 (including brainlife.io's S3 buckets), you’ll find a directory structure containing various .z* files that specify metadata, multiscale images, and associated attributes. Here’s an example of what an OME-Zarr layout might look like: - .zattrs and .zgroup store high-level metadata about the dataset. - The numbered directories (0, 1, etc.) represent different resolutions or scales of the image data. - Each .zarray contains metadata for that specific resolution level. - The numbered files within each resolution directory (for example, 0, 1, 2) contain the actual chunked pixel data. When working with OME-Zarr data on S3, you can use tools such as zarr-python or ome-zarr-py to read and write image data directly from the bucket.

The goal of this tutorial is to process anatomical and diffusion data to: Generate ACPC alignment and non-linear warp fields to the MNI152 template. Map these microstructural metrics directly onto the 2D gray/white cortical interface. * Extract regional summary statistics across cortical parcellations (Destrieux Atlas aparc.a2009s). This tutorial demonstrates the standard steps used to preprocess diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (dMRI) data on brainlife.io (connects.brainlife.io ). The goal of this tutorial is to process raw diffusion MRI scans and anatomical images into high-quality, analysis-ready outputs for: Microstructural modeling (Diffusion Tensor Imaging: FA, MD, RD, AD; and advanced NODDI models) Whole-brain diffusion tractography (streamline reconstruction) * Structural network neuroscience (connectomics and white matter mapping) This pipeline primarily uses MRtrix3 Preproc for comprehensive diffusion artifact correction and FSL DTIFit for microstructural tensor modeling. This tutorial builds on skills developed in the Introduction to brainlife.io and Anatomical Preprocessing tutorials. ---

To ensure that all downstream diffusion measures and tractography streamlines are biologically and anatomically anchored, the high-resolution T1-weighted image must be linearly aligned to the Anterior Commissure - Posterior Commissure (ACPC) plane. This is accomplished using FSL Anat (T1) .

Diffusion MRI data has a relatively low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and is sensitive to several physical artifacts during rapid echo-planar imaging (EPI): Thermal Noise: Thermal fluctuations create high-frequency noise. MRtrix3 uses Marchenko-Pastur Principal Component Analysis (MP-PCA) and Rician estimation to suppress noise while preserving spatial resolution. Gibbs Ringing: Truncation in k-space acquisition causes oscillatory "ringing" artifacts near sharp tissue borders. Sub-voxel shifts remove these artifacts. Susceptibility Distortions & Eddy Currents: Rapid gradient switching induces electrical currents in the scanner bore (eddy currents), while air-tissue boundaries warp magnetic fields. Using reverse phase-encoded pairs (e.g. Posterior-to-Anterior PA and Anterior-to-Posterior AP), FSL topup and eddy model and correct these geometric distortions. Coregistration: Finally, the preprocessed dMRI volume is rigidly aligned to the ACPC-aligned T1w image.

Once cleaned and aligned, the Diffusion Tensor (DTI) model is fit to the data: Fractional Anisotropy (FA): Measures the degree of directional organization of water diffusion (from 0 for isotropic fluid like CSF to 1 for highly aligned white matter tracts). Mean Diffusivity (MD): Total average diffusion across all directions. * Axial Diffusivity (AD) & Radial Diffusivity (RD): Diffusion along the primary fiber orientation vs. perpendicular to it. ---

section: Diffusion Tractography and White Matter Tractometry
content: This tutorial demonstrates the standard pipeline used to perform whole-brain diffusion tractography, major white matter tract segmentation, and tractometry analysis on brainlife.io (connects.brainlife.io ). The goal of this tutorial is to process anatomical and diffusion MRI data to: Generate whole-brain tractograms using Constrained Spherical Deconvolution (CSD) and Anatomically-Constrained Tractography (ACT). Segment major white matter tracts (such as the Arcuate Fasciculus, Corticospinal Tract, and Corpus Callosum) with automated anatomical segmentation. Remove outlier streamlines to isolate biologically plausible tract cores. Map microstructural profiles (tractometry) along each tract's length for group statistical comparisons. This tutorial builds on concepts from the Introduction to brainlife.io, Anatomical Preprocessing, and Diffusion MRI Preprocessing tutorials. ---

pageTitle: Diffusion Tractography and White Matter Tractometry
Diffusion Tractography and White Matter Tractometry
content: Unlike simple tensor models that assume only a single fiber orientation per voxel, Constrained Spherical Deconvolution (CSD) estimates the continuous fiber orientation distribution function (fODF). This allows tractography algorithms to track through complex regions of crossing, kissing, and branching fibers. Anatomically-Constrained Tractography (ACT) utilizes FreeSurfer tissue boundaries (5TT segmentation) to ensure streamlines begin and terminate only in gray matter and do not traverse cerebrospinal fluid.

This reveals localized focal differences between clinical cohorts. ---

This page provides a simple tutorial for using ezBIDS. The goal of this tutorial is to demonstrate how to use ezBIDS in order to convert imaging data to BIDS. For more in-depth information regarding the functionality and features of ezBIDS, please refer to the user documentation. This tutorial converts MRI. ezBIDS on the web also converts PET and MEG; EEG, iEEG, NIRS, EMG and microscopy are imported on your own computer with aimport. Before we begin, we'll need some test data, which can be found here. After a few minutes, the data will be downloaded to your Downloads folder, titled "ezBIDStutorialdata".

Here is a tree structure of the downloaded data: As you can see, we have a standard collection of MRI data and corresponding timing data for two subjects. The MRI data in the data folder includes localizers, anatomical T1w, spin-echo field maps, and functional BOLD (and SBRef) sequences. The logs folder contains timing data corresponding to the runs of the bart task from each subject's scans. This sample data contains NIfTI/JSON file pairs rather than the raw DICOMs themselves. ezBIDS accepts either option (DICOMs, NIfTI/JSON) when uploading data.

Now, we are ready to use ezBIDS. All you need is a web browser (Chrome or Firefox preferred) and an internet connection. Copy and paste the ezBIDS URL (https://brainlife.io/ezbids) into your web browser. For a companion video that follows this documentation, see our ezBIDS tutorial video.

Upon reaching the ezBIDS homepage, click "LOG IN/REGISTER" in the upper right part of the web page to sign into your brainlife.io account. If you do not have a brainlife.io account, you will be guided through a quick setup. This process is simple and meant for authentication purposes. If you are already logged into your brainlife.io account, you will instead see and click "GET STARTED".

Click the "Choose Files" (or "Browse") button and select the data folder to upload the imaging data. We will upload the logs folder later. The tutorial should be in your Downloads folder, titled "ezBIDStutorialdata". This upload process may take a couple of minutes, depending on the strength of your internet connection. Once uploaded, you will see some text generated on the screen, indicating that ezBIDS is performing several automated, behind-the-scenes processes to extract as much relevant BIDS information about your dataset as possible. This is meant to save you time later on. Once complete, you will see text reading "Analysis complete!" along with a list of your uploaded imaging data. From here, ezBIDS will guide you through several steps for you to verify and make any corrections or modifications to ensure that the data is specified to your liking. Importantly, ezBIDS will alert you to any details that need to be addressed in order to ensure BIDS compliance.

This page allows you to specify information about the entire dataset. Notice how ezBIDS will autofill several fields for you. Required fields have been marked with a red asterisk, indicating that this information is absolutely needed to have a BIDS-compliant dataset. However, the information that ezBIDS provides may not always be appropriate, necessitating changes if you so choose. For example, the Dataset Name is specified as Untitled, which isn't very informative. Let's change that field instead to myDataset. Additionally, the Authors field is currently blank since ezBIDS couldn't determine that information, and it's not a required field for BIDS compliance. Select the Authors field, type your name (e.g. John Doe), and press the Return (or Enter) button on your keyboard. You are more than welcome to provide additional information on this page, but for this tutorial, we will move on by clicking the "Next" button at the bottom right side of the web page.

This page allows you to verify or modify the subject (and session) IDs for your data. ezBIDS provided the correct subject IDs (01, 02), but you may modify them if you like. For the purpose of this tutorial, though, let's leave them as they are. Note that the session fields for each subject are left blank. A session ID denotes that an individual subject was scanned multiple times. This field should thus remain empty unless the individual subjects were scanned more than once during separate visits. In the case of our data, each subject was scanned only once, and thus no session ID should be specified. Since ezBIDS specified the correct subject IDs, we can click the "Next" button to proceed.

This page allows you to verify and modify the imaging data identity, as well as provide additional information that will better describe the dataset. You will notice on the left side of the page that the data has been labeled and grouped into a list of "like-minded" groups, specified by a group ID value (e.g. #1). The purpose of this grouping is to organize data that are the same but collected across separate subjects (or sessions). For example, each subject has an anatomical T1w sequence collected containing the same scan parameters, so ezBIDS groups these two sequences together for now. The number of sequences in each group is also provided (e.g. 2 objs). When you make a modification to a group, it will be applied to all files in the group. Thereby saving you time having to modify each sequence individually, though that is an option later on. It is best practice to make as many necessary edits on this page as possible. On upcoming pages, you can see the changes for each file and make more surgical changes then. Note that the data have been identified with a specific datatype and suffix pairing (e.g. the anatomical T1w data group is specified as anat/T1w). This is how BIDS standardizes the identity of data. For example, this is anatomical (anat) data, but more specifically, it is a T1w sequence. Any additional labeling information for the data (known as "entities" in BIDS parlance) is also provided if ezBIDS detects it. For example, the functional BOLD and SBRef data (func/b

We will now upload the timing files in the logs directory of our tutorial data. Simply click the "Select File(s)" (or "Browse") button and specify the logs directory (you will upload all contents in there) in your "ezBIDStutorialdata" folder. You will then see a list of header fields on the left (Onset, Duration, etc) with a corresponding drop-down menu. This is ezBIDS's way of asking you to specify which columns in the timing files correspond to the header fields on the left. For Onset, choose tstart, and for Duration choose dur. These two headers are the only required fields to proceed; the rest are optional and can be left empty for this tutorial.

On this page, you will see all your data labeled and organized by subject ID and in order of when they were collected during the scan. Notably, the grouping has been removed so every sequence can be examined individually. Note that the acquisition-mprage addition we made back on the Series Mapping page has been applied to each anat/T1w sequence. You will also notice that the timing files have been identified as func/events and contain the same entity labels as their corresponding func/bold sequences (i.e. task-bart). Additionally, the func/events are placed directly underneath their corresponding func/bold, to better visualize the correspondence. As always, you are able to modify things as you see fit, but for this tutorial, everything appears to be in good order (i.e. no errors or warnings) so we will proceed.

This page allows you to deface (i.e. remove) the facial features from every anatomical (anat) sequence in the uploaded data, by selecting an option in the Defacing Method drop-down menu. The recommended option is to use the quickshear package because it is relatively quick and effective; however, you may choose the pydeface package instead. Once a defacing procedure is selected, a screenshot of the original (un-defaced) data is shown on the left. Once defacing is complete, a screenshot of the defaced image is provided on the right, allowing you to see the quality of the resulting defacing. If the defacing is bad (i.e. part of the brain has been cut) you can either select the other defacing option or simply forgo defacing for that specific anatomical sequence. If you choose the latter in this situation, select the "Use Original" button above the original screenshot. Defacing is an optional procedure, so you can skip this step if you so choose. However, it is highly recommended that you perform defacing to remove identifying information. This form of anonymization is particularly important if you plan on sharing data with colleagues or the broader imaging community.

This page allows you to specify phenotype data pertaining to each subject. By default, ezBIDS will attempt to extract and provide the sex and age information, and you may include additional phenotype information if you wish (e.g. handedness experiment_group, etc) or even remove fields. In this example, ezBIDS was unable to determine the sex and age of the two subjects because this information could not be found in the data. It is generally good practice to provide some level of phenotypical information, thus, for sub-01, set the sex and age as M and 30 respectively. For sub-02 do F and 26.

Upon reaching this page, you've completed all the ezBIDS steps. What you'll now do is click on the green Finalize button so that ezBIDS can apply all the edits and modifications you made earlier. The result should be a dataset that is properly organized and labeled according to BIDS. If you do not wish for the previously excluded data to be included in the BIDS dataset (by default it gets placed in an excluded folder) you can uncheck the blue checkmark above the Finalize button. Once finalized, you will see two boxes underneath. On the left is the BIDS Structure, which provides a tree structure of your BIDS data (notice the differences in this output compared to what we started with at the beginning of this tutorial). On the right is the bids-validator output, which runs the BIDS-validator as a final assessment to see whether your data is BIDS-compliant (i.e. passes validation). If any red text is present in the bids-validator output, this means that your data is NOT BIDS-compliant and requires some additional work. In such cases, you might need to go back a few pages to correct the error(s). Once you return to this page, click the Rerun Finalize Step to apply your new changes. If any gold text is present, this means that there is a warning and should be corrected, but you do not necessarily have to. You still have a BIDS-compliant dataset! This tutorial demonstrates standard steps used to preprocess functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data on brainlife.io (connects.brainlife.io ). The goal of this tutorial is to process raw BOLD fMRI scans and structural data into analysis-ready outputs for: Functional activation & region-of-interest (ROI) analysis Functional connectivity network matrices (measuring synchronous BOLD signal correlations across brain networks) You will use fMRIPrep (fMRIPrep - Volume Output ) on brainlife.io. This tutorial builds on concepts from the Introduction to brainlife.io and Anatomical Preprocessing tutorials. ---
Processing functional MRI involves three core stages:

Before functional images can be properly interpreted, they must be registered to high-resolution structural images. Standardizing orientation and centering the brain to the Anterior Commissure - Posterior Commissure (ACPC) plane is accomplished with the FSL Anat (T1) and FSL Anat (T2) Apps. Cortical surfaces are subsequently reconstructed with FreeSurfer 7.3.2 .

Functional BOLD scans suffer from several common acquisition artifacts: Head Motion: Participant motion during scan acquisition shifts voxels across volumes. fMRIPrep estimates head movement (translations and rotations) across all frames and realigns the volumes. B0 Susceptibility Distortions: Differences in magnetic susceptibility between brain tissue and air cavities cause geometric distortions ("stretching" or "compression" in frontal/temporal lobes). fMRIPrep uses phase-encoding fieldmaps (fmap) to unwarp distortions. Slice-Timing Differences: 2D multislice sequences acquire brain slices sequentially rather than instantaneously. Slice-timing correction interpolates the temporal signal so all slices reflect the same effective timepoint. Coregistration: Functional volumes are rigidly registered to the subject's high-resolution T1w anatomical surface and transformed into standardized space (e.g. MNI152). ---

Welcome to brainlife.io (connects.brainlife.io ). brainlife.io is a free, open platform for brain data across scales: you bring data into a project, run reproducible analyses as Apps on shared supercomputers, look at the results in your browser, and publish them with a DOI. Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) measures the Blood Oxygen Level-Dependent (BOLD) signal across the whole brain over time. Functional connectivity characterizes how synchronized the spontaneous or task-evoked BOLD activity is between distinct brain regions. Brain regions whose BOLD timeseries exhibit strong temporal correlation are inferred to form functionally integrated networks. These correlations are typically represented in an $N \times N$ functional connectivity matrix (correlation matrix), where each entry $(i, j)$ contains the Pearson correlation coefficient between the mean timeseries of region $i$ and region $j$, defined by a cortical or subcortical atlas. From these matrices, neuroscientists can characterize topological properties of the functional connectome (such as resting-state subnetworks, modularity, hub architecture, and dynamic flexibility) across tasks, age groups, and clinical populations. This tutorial demonstrates how to generate functional connectivity matrices on brainlife.io (connects.brainlife.io). You will learn how to: 1. Align anatomical T1w images to ACPC space using FSL Anat. 2. Reconstruct cortical surfaces and parcellations using FreeSurfer 7.3.2. 3. Map the HCP-MMP (Glasser 180-node) cortical atlas onto native surfaces with the Multi-atlas Transfer Tool (MaTT). 4. Preprocess resting-state BOLD images using fMRIPrep (Volume Output). 5. Extract regional BOLD timeseries using fMRI Timeseries Extraction. 6. Compute correlation matric

Anatomical alignment to the Anterior Commissure - Posterior Commissure (ACPC) plane is performed first via FSL Anat (T1w). This provides a centered, robust anatomical reference for surface reconstruction in FreeSurfer 7.3.2 and boundary-based registration in fMRIPrep. The Glasser multi-modal cortical parcellation (hcp-mmp-b) is mapped to the subject's native anatomy using the Multi-atlas Transfer Tool (MaTT), producing the region-of-interest (ROI) volume used for timeseries extraction.

Raw fMRI data is prone to head motion artifacts, slice acquisition delays, and magnetic susceptibility distortions. fMRIPrep performs: - Head-motion estimation and slice-timing correction. - Susceptibility distortion correction (fieldmaps or phase-difference images). - Boundary-Based Registration (BBR) aligning the BOLD volumes to the anatomical T1w space. - Extraction of confound regressors (FD, DVARS, CSF/WM physiological signals, anatomical CompCor).

Following fMRIPrep: - The fMRI Timeseries Extraction App applies the cortical atlas mask to the preprocessed BOLD data, averages the timeseries across voxels within each parcel, and regresses out motion confounds. - The Time series to network App computes the pairwise Pearson correlation matrix across all parcel timeseries. - Network preprocessing and graph measurements quantify community structure, clustering, path lengths, and node centralities. ---
