Let's start by learning a little bit about structural connectivity. Diffusion MRI measures how anisotropic the movement of water is, with the basic principle that myelinated axon bundles restrict water displacement preferentially along the direction of the fibers. Structural connectivity describes the structural organization of white matter pathways across the entire brain. This analysis characterizes how connected different brain regions are by computing the density and number of diffusion tractography streamlines that connect or terminate into pairs of regions. These connectivity values are stored in a connectivity matrix (or adjacency matrix), where each cell $(i, j)$ represents the structural connection weight between region $i$ and region $j$ defined by an anatomical atlas. From these matrices, neuroscientists can apply graph theory to examine network-level topological properties such as global efficiency, modularity, node degree, and clustering coefficient, revealing inter-individual differences in development, aging, and clinical disorders. This tutorial demonstrates how to generate structural connectivity matrices on brainlife.io (connects.brainlife.io). You will learn how to: 1. Align anatomical images to ACPC space using FSL Anat. 2. Reconstruct cortical surfaces and parcellations using FreeSurfer 7.3.2. 3. Map the Glasser 180-node multi-modal cortical parcellation (HCP-MMP 1.0) using Multi-atlas Transfer Tool (MaTT). 4. Preprocess raw diffusion MRI data with MRtrix

Anatomical images (T1w and T2w) serve as the spatial reference frame for diffusion tractography. To ensure that streamline endpoints match biological cortical boundaries, our anatomical volumes must be rigidly aligned to the Anterior Commissure - Posterior Commissure (ACPC) plane. This centering and standard orientation step is executed using FSL Anat. Next, cortical surfaces and subcortical segmentations are reconstructed using FreeSurfer 7.3.2. The resulting surfaces allow us to project high-resolution parcellation schemes (such as Glasser HCP-MMP) onto each subject's native anatomy using the Multi-atlas Transfer Tool (MaTT).

Diffusion MRI datasets inherently suffer from several scanner artifacts: - Susceptibility distortions: Geometric stretching and compression caused by $B0$ field inhomogeneities at air-tissue interfaces. - Eddy currents and subject motion: Phase distortions and misalignment induced by fast gradient switching and inevitable head movements. - Low Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) and Rician noise floor. - Gibbs ringing: Spurious oscillations adjacent to sharp tissue boundaries. - $B1$ field bias inhomogeneities: Low-frequency intensity variations across the image volume. The MRtrix3 Preproc (DESIGNER) App performs MP-PCA denoising, Gibbs deringing, FSL topup susceptibility distortion correction, FSL eddy motion/eddy current correction, and $B_1$ bias field correction, followed by rigid registration of the dMRI volume to the ACPC-aligned T1w image.

Once dMRI data is cleaned and aligned to the T1w space, we model white matter fiber orientation distributions using Constrained Spherical Deconvolution (CSD). Unlike single-tensor models, CSD resolves complex fiber architectures including crossing, kissing, and diverging axon fascicles within a single voxel. Using the CSD fiber orientation distributions and a 5-tissue-type (5TT) anatomical segmentation derived from FreeSurfer, the MRtrix3 ACT algorithm generates millions of anatomically valid streamlines. ACT dynamically terminates streamlines that cross into cerebrospinal fluid or exit through gray matter boundaries, eliminating biologically implausible connections.

With our whole-brain tractogram and the Glasser 180-node cortical parcellation volume aligned in native space, the Structural Connectome MRtrix3 (SCMRT) App maps streamline endpoints to pairs of atlas regions. It computes: - Streamline count (density): The raw and length-normalized number of streamlines connecting region $i$ to region $j$. - Microstructural weighting: Connecting matrices weighted by mean fractional anisotropy (FA), mean diffusivity (MD), or tract length. ---

section: Ensemble tractography Single-Shell Diffusion and Tractography Processing.
content: The goal of this pipeline is to process dMRI and T1w data to generate tract profiles using the Diffusion Tensor (DTI) model. This pipeline combines processing proposed by Caiafa and Pestilli, Scientific Reports (2017), Yeatman et al., PloS One (2012), and Takemura et al., PLoS Computational Biology (2016). The pipeline is optimized for single-shell dMRI data and should not be used for multishell data. 1. Brain Parcellation (FreeSurfer). The first step is to launch FreeSurfer, this will perform anatomical preprocessing and parcellate the brain into different regions: https://doi.org/10.25663/bl.app.0 2. Diffusion MRI Preprocessing (VISTASOFT). A commonly used pipeline for dMRI processing is called dtiInit. Originally developed by VistaLab at Stanford Universty, this processing will align the dMRI data to the T1w data, reorient the BVECS accordingly, remove motion artifacts, and reduce Eddy- Current artifacts. https://doi.org/10.25663/bl.app.3 3. Generate Diffusion Tensor Model data. Once the dMRI data have been processed, we need to generate the parameters for the DTI model. These were generated in the previous step. The following app extracts the parameters and makes them available to build tract profiles. https://doi.org/10.25663/bl.app.48 4. Tractography (Ensemble Tractography). section: Ensemble tractography Multishell Diffusion Processing using DESIGNER
content: Today, some of the most common dMRI data are acquired with multiple shells. This allows fitting models to the diffusion signal with additional parameters to better capture the complexity of the signal in areas of fiber crossing. Networks, broadly, describe how centers (i.e. nodes) of a mechanism interact with one another and are connected (i.e. edges). One example of a network is the internet, with computers connecting to, and sharing information amongst, each other. Specifically in neuroscience, these networks describe how specific cortical regions in the brain are connected, either in terms of correlated BOLD signal (fMRI) or streamline density (dMRI). From this information, it’s possible to model how the brain is organized, both on global and local scales. For example, Sporns et al (2000) were able to model the organization of the white matter connections in the macaque visual cortex, providing supporting evidence of specific anatomical subgroupings within the visual cortex. This information is stored in the form of a matrix, with each cell in the matrix corresponding to the connectivity between two specific cortical regions. Specifically, these matrices can expresses either the presence of a connection (i.e. binary network) or the strength of a connection (i.e. weighted network). The data in these matrices can be viewed in multiple graphical ways which may illuminate specific communities, or interconnected regions within the global network, that might not be readily present in the matrix.

Functional MRI measures the BOLD signal - a measure associated with neuronal activity - across the entire brain in order to identify functional characteristics of the brain. One particular type of analysis that describes the functional organization of the brain is functional connectivity analysis. Functional connectivity characterizes how in-sync, or out-of-sync, particular regions are by correlating their BOLD responses at every time point across an entire fMRI scan. The rationale is that regions that are highly correlated in their BOLD responses at a given time are likely to be working together for a particular task or activity. These correlation values are stored in what is known as a connectivity matrix. Each position in the matrix represents the correlation of BOLD activity between two particular regions. From these matrices, scientists can then examine properties that describe the inter-relatedness of many regions. These properties can be used to identify functional network-level inter-individual differences in a large cohort.

Diffusion MRI measures how anistropic the movement of water is, with the basic principle that myelinated tissue will create more anistropic water movement.. One particular type of analysis that describes the structural organization of the white matter using this data is structural connectivity. Structural connectivity characterizes connected different regions are by computing the number of diffusion tractography streamlines that terminate into a particular region. The rationale is that regions that have greater density of streamline terminations have greater connectivity with the regions where those streamlines also terminate. These density values are stored in what is known as a connectivity matrix. Each position in the matrix represents the connectivity between two particular regions. From these matrices, scientists can then examine properties that describe the inter-relatedness of many regions. These properties can be used to identify structural network-level inter-individual differences in a large cohort. This page demonstrates how to generate both functional and structural connectivity matrices on brainlife.io. The goal of this tutorial is to show you how to generate functional and structural connectivity matrices following anatomical (T1w), fMRI, and dMRI preprocessing. This tutorial will use a combination of skills developed in the Introduction tutorial, Anatomical (T1w) Preprocessing, fMRI Preprocessing, and the dMRI Preprocessing tutorials. If you are not comfortable

The first step of structural network generation often involves processing the anatomical images. In order to guarantee that any generalizations regarding location made from the preprocessed diffusion data is anatomically-informed, we must have both of our anatomical (T1w or T2w) images and our functional and diffusion MRI images aligned. One way we can make this easier for fMRIPrep and MRTrix3 Preprocessing is by aligning the anatomical images in such a way that center of the brain is centered in the image. We refer to this as ACPC-aligned, as we are aligning the data to the anterior commissure-posterior comissure plane. This is the first step in fMRI & dMRI preprocessing, and is typically done with the FSL Anat (T1w) app. In order to map the Glasser 180-node atlas using the Multi-atlas Transfer Tool (MaTT) and compute the streamline density between each region, we first need to generate cortical and white matter surfaces, and brain region parcellations, using Freesurfer. Once our anatomical image is aligned, our surfaces are generated, and the Glasser 180-node cortical atlas is mapped, we can move onto functional and diffusion preprocessing.

The second step of the networks workflow involves processing the functional (fMRI) images. These can include both task-related (a person performing a task in the scanner) or resting-state (a person does no task in the scanner) fMRIs. Like any image directly from the scanner, there are common artifacts and issues with fMRI data. One of the biggest problems is motion. Because some scans take a long time, it is nearly impossible for a participant to lie completely motionless. Even the most subtle movements can alter the results in a specific region and make your data less accurate. fMRIPrep will estimate the motion that occurred across all of the fMRI volumes and correct for it. This will align all of the volumes perfectly to ensure motion is not altering the data. Another common artifact in fMRI data is susceptibility distortions. This is when regions of the brain look "wavy" or fold inward or outward on itself in images. This is due to how the scanner sweeps across the entire brain during acquisition -- fMRIPrep will also automatically correct for this! fMRIPrep can additionally fix the lag in the BOLD signal and the fact that we need to acquire data in non-contiguous slices. This is referred to as slice-timing, or the order in which slices are acquired. Without fMRIPrep, our data would not be ordered properly and we wouldn't have contiguous brain slices. Finally, images from the fMRI scanner might not be perfectly aligned to images collected before it, such as the anatomical

Once the anatomical and fMRI data is preprocessed with fMRIPrep, we can now examine the functional network organization by generating functional connectivity matrices! This is done by examining the fMRI BOLD activity in multiple regions across the brain by correlating the regions' BOLD activity throughout the entire acquisition. The reason we do this is because regions that are active in similar ways at similar time points are more likely to be working with each other to perform a specific task. The way we typically represent the correlation coefficients, or weights, of each region (node) with every other region (node) in the brain is with a network matrix -- note that nodes represent the brain regions here. Each point in the network matrix represents the correlation of BOLD activity between one region and another. We can then use these network matrices to examine properties of the network that describe how interrelated specific regions in the brain are working during the fMRI acquisition in either task-related or resting-state fMRIs.

The next step after anatomical and functional preprocessing is to preprocess the diffusion data. dMRI data, like any other MRI dataset, is quite noisy. Just like fMRI, dMRI data is sensitive to susceptibility distortions. This is when regions of the brain look "wavy" or fold inward or outward on itself in images. This is due to how the scanner sweeps across the entire brain during acquisition. Also, dMRI data is very susceptible to motion. Because some scans take a long time, it is nearly impossible for a participant to lie completely motionless. Even the most subtle movements can alter the results in a specific region and make your data less accurate. Finally, movement of the magnetic gradients can induce electromagnetic currents which can affect the measurement in any given location. This is called eddy currents, and is due to the fact that electricity and magnetism are part of the same field - i.e. the electromagnetic field. We can correct for all of these common artifacts using MRTrix3 Preprocessing. In addition to these artifacts, dMRI has very low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), which directly impacts how well you can fit microstructural models and analyze diffusion data. This means that in any given location, the amount of diffusion signal is very low compared to the "noise" of the scanner. There are methods to lower the amount of noise across the brain, and thus increase the SNR. MRTrix3 Preprocessing has the capability to identify and remove noise using principal compon

Once the dMRI data has been cleaned and aligned to the anatomical (T1w) image, the next step is to map the underlying white matter anatomy using diffusion tractography. Diffusion tractography works by modelling how water is moving throughout the brain based on the principle of anisotropy -- that water will move unequally in a particular direction given a physical constraint. In the case of diffusion MRI, this constraint comes from the myelin wrapping the many axons arranged into bundles known as fasicles. There are common groupings of these fasicles, known as white matter tracts, based on their terminations into the cortex. Diffusion tractography generates streamlines that act as evidence of underlying white matter organization. We can bundle these streamlines into common white matter tracts digitally, just as we can bundle fasciles into tracts using histological methods. The first step is to fit models of diffusion at each location in the dMRI image that can be used as a guide for the tractography algorithms. The most popular model for this is known as constrained spherical deconvolution, or CSD. CSD allows for the possibility of multiple fasicles entering a single location that may have different trajectories, which is a major advantage of the model over other models of diffusion. The CSD model at each location can tell the tracking algorithm how strongly and in what direction water is diffusing in the brain, and thus where organized and myelinated white matter is likely to

Once the whole-brain tractograms have been generated, we can now compute the streamline density between each region and generate our structural connectivity matrices. These matrices can then be used to derive network-related measures of the white matter organization of an individual or of common properties amongst groups. For this tutorial, we will use network matrices to generate our structural connectivity matrix. Now, let's get to work! The following steps of this tutorial will show you how to: 1. ACPC-align the anatomical (T1w) image, 1. Generate Freesurfer surfaces and parcellations, 1. Map Glasser 180-node cortical atlas to the surface, 1. Preprocess fMRI data 1. Preprocess dMRI data, 1. Perform diffusion tractography, 1. and generate network matrices (functional and structural) from the regions of the Glasser 180-node atlas.

section: Identify the effects of concussion on the volumes of brain tissue - Anatomical Preprocessing.
content: As a structural neuroimager and neuroscientist, I am interested in how structural properties of the brain relate to behavior or disease. For example, I am interested in how concussions may affect the volume of the motor cortex, the primary visual cortex, the hippocampus, and prefrontal cortex and how that relates to behavior. I want to know: 1) how concussions affect the volume of these structures, 2) are different tissue types affected differentially from concussions, and 3) how these alterations relate to behavior. In order to answer these questions, I need to compare measures derived from concussed athletes with a healthy control population in order to identify any concussion-specific effects on brain tissue. These questions are important to understanding the effects of concussions and may be useful in identifying markers that can predict whether or not a person has a concussion. To answer these questions, I will need a specific type of MRI image: an anatomical T1w image. I then need to preprocess this data in a specific way in order to measure the volumes of the structures of interest in an accurate and reliable way. FreeSurfer 7.3.2 : Reconstructs the underlying cortical surfaces required for retinotopic mapping. This tutorial builds on concepts from the Introduction to brainlife.io and Anatomical Preprocessing tutorials. ---
Retinotopy is the spatial preservation of the visual field from the retina through the lateral geniculate nucleus to the primary visual cortex (V1) and higher visual areas (V2, V3, hV4).

Functional retinotopy experiments require specialized visual display setups and prolonged MRI scan sessions. Atlas-based Bayesian retinotopic mapping algorithms (Benson et al., 2014, PLOS Computational Biology) predict individual retinotopic maps with high biological fidelity solely from the subject's cortical anatomy and sulcal geometry. ---

This tutorial demonstrates the standard steps used to preprocess anatomical magnetic resonance imaging data (T1-weighted or T1w) on brainlife.io (connects.brainlife.io ). The goal of this tutorial is to process raw anatomical MRI scans into standardized, analysis-ready outputs for: - Volumetric and morphometric analyses (cortical thickness, surface area, and subcortical volumes). - Multi-modal coregistration needed for downstream diffusion MRI (dMRI / tractography) or functional MRI (fMRI) pipelines. This tutorial builds on the Getting Started guide. ---
Processing a T1-weighted image involves four standard stages:

Raw anatomical images can vary considerably in head orientation, field of view, and acquisition artifacts across different MRI scanners. Standardizing orientation ensures that voxels are indexed correctly across neuroimaging toolboxes (with the brain upright, nose pointing right in sagittal views, and facing forward in axial/coronal views). Next, the brain is aligned to the Anterior Commissure - Posterior Commissure (ACPC) plane. Linearly aligning the T1w image to a standard reference template (e.g., MNI152) centers the coordinates and aligns the interhemispheric fissure. This alignment is required by downstream tools such as FreeSurfer. On brainlife.io, the FSL Anat (T1) App does all of this.

Once ACPC-aligned, FreeSurfer 7.3.2 segments the brain into tissue classes (cerebral white matter, cortical gray matter, and subcortical structures) and reconstructs smooth 2D mesh models of the pial surface and white matter boundary. FreeSurfer also segments hippocampal subfields and thalamic nuclei, yielding parcellations used in structural connectivity and morphometry.

While FreeSurfer generates standard segmentations (such as Desikan-Killiany and DKT), modern connectomics often requires fine-grained multi-modal parcellations. The Multi-Atlas Transfer Tool (maTT) maps specialized atlases—such as the Glasser Human Connectome Project Multi-Modal Parcellation (hcp-mmp-b) or the Yeo 17 resting-state networks—directly onto the subject's reconstructed cortical surface.

Finally, morphological metrics (surface vertex count, surface area, cortical thickness, volume, and curvature) are collated across each region of interest (ROI) into standardized .csv spreadsheets using Compute Anatomical Statistics (or FreeSurfer Statistics). These tables feed directly into group-level statistical models. ---

section: Step 4: FreeSurfer Surface Reconstruction and Parcellation
content: With the ACPC-aligned T1w data ready, run FreeSurfer: 1. Open your process: go to 3. Processing → Processes, select the process, and choose Editor in its side panel. Then select Add App. 2. Select App: search for Freesurfer 7.3.2 and select it. 3. Configure App Settings: - hippocampal: on, to segment hippocampal subfields. - thalamicnuclei: on, to segment individual thalamic nuclei. 4. When the job finishes, select Visualize on the FreeSurfer output and choose freeview. It loads the cortical surfaces (pial and white matter), subcortical segmentations (aseg) and volumetric parcellations in your browser. ---

section: Step 5: Map the Multimodal Atlas (Multi-Atlas Transfer Tool)

Select App: search for Multi-Atlas Transfer Tool (maTT) and select it. 3. Configure App Settings: for atlas, select hcp-mmp-b. 4. Select Inputs: for freesurfer, choose the FreeSurfer output from Step 4. 5. Configure Outputs: keep Archive Output on, then select Add App. This step projects the HCP multimodal parcellation onto the subject's cortical surfaces and outputs parcellated surface files and annotation files. ---

The final processing step extracts ROI-by-ROI morphometric statistics into analysis-ready summary tables: 1. In the process editor, select Add App. 2. Select App: search for Compute Anatomical Statistics (or FreeSurfer Statistics) and select it. 3. Select Inputs: - freesurfer: choose the FreeSurfer output from Step 4. - parcsurface and parcsurf_vertices: choose the outputs of the Multi-Atlas Transfer Tool from Step 5. 4. Configure Outputs: keep Archive Output on, then select Add App. When the job finishes, it outputs summary .csv files containing cortical thickness, surface area, and volume across all anatomical ROIs. ---

Select New analysis, choose a notebook from Blank Template Notebooks, and select Create to launch a Jupyter notebook in your browser. 3. Load the generated .csv files using pandas: 4. Perform ANOVA, linear regressions, or plot regional cortical thickness distributions across subjects and groups in the notebook. ---

pageTitle: Clairvoy Tutorial: Clinical Concussion Risk Prediction
content: Clairvoy is an automated clinical research application hosted on brainlife.io. The Clairvoy App utilizes a machine learning classifier to predict whether an individual who has sustained a concussion is at high risk for prolonged symptoms or slow recovery (defined as the lack of clinical clearance for full return to sports/daily activity at >28 days). The underlying machine learning model evaluates diffusion-weighted (dMRI) and T1-weighted structural MRI acquired within 24–48 hours post-injury. This experimental tool is based on peer-reviewed research by Bertó et al. 2024 (NeuroImage: Clinical, 43, 103646). > [!IMPORTANT] Investigational Use Only > Clairvoy was developed with support from the U.S. Department of Defense (award W81XWH-20-1-0717, PI: Nicholas L. Port) and the NCAA/DOD CARE Consortium (award W81XWH-14-2-0151, PI: Thomas W. McAllister). Clairvoy is an open-science research tool and has not yet received FDA clearance or validation as a standalone diagnostic medical device. We welcome clinical researchers and neuroscientists to evaluate Clairvoy and provide feedback. ---

pageTitle: Clairvoy Tutorial: Clinical Concussion Risk Prediction
content: Clairvoy couples the browser-based ezBIDS conversion service with automated pipelines on brainlife.io: 1. ezBIDS: Ingests raw DICOM or NIfTI series, automatically identifies imaging sequences, defaces anatomical images for participant privacy, and generates a valid BIDS-compliant dataset. 2. Apps on brainlife.io do not exchange arbitrary files. They exchange datatypes. A datatype specifies which files and folders a dataset contains, so that "Apps process data, taking in specific datatypes as input and producing resulting datatypes." Because Apps agree on datatypes, the output of one App can be the input of another, even when the two Apps wrap different software (for example FSL, FreeSurfer, MRtrix3 or ANTs). ---

A datatype has a name (for example neuro/anat/t1w or neuro/dwi), a description, and a list of the files and folders a dataset of that type contains. For example, a neuro/dwi dataset contains dwi.nii.gz, dwi.bvecs and dwi.bvals. The definition is stored as JSON. This example, for the neuro/life datatype, lists two files and one folder:

Datatypes and BIDS both standardize data, for different purposes: - BIDS organizes a whole dataset on disk: folders, subjects, sessions and metadata. - Datatypes describe one item of data, raw or derived, so that an App receives exactly the files it expects, whoever produced them. ---

- Datatypes (sidebar, under Explore): the catalog of all datatypes. - My Datatypes: datatypes you administer. Search by name or description, and filter by Supports validation (the datatype has a validator that checks new datasets) or Supports Jupyter notebooks. A datatype's page shows: - About: what the datatype is. - Files & directories: the files and folders a dataset of this type contains. - Official tags: the datatype tags officially supported for this datatype. - Apps: Apps that take this datatype as input or produce it as output. - Maintainers, Sample Data and Visualizers: who maintains the datatype, example datasets, and the viewers that can open it. - Upload Instructions: how to upload data of this type with the command-line tool. To create a datatype, open My Datatypes, select Datatype (the button with a plus sign), enter a Name and Description, and select Create datatype. You can add files, tags and a validator after it is created. ---

In the app, filters are labeled Datatype and Annotations, and a pipeline uses "Filter by Datatype Tag" and "Filter by Annotation" to resolve ambiguous inputs. ---

A job (one run of one App) can fail because of a wrong setting, unsuitable input data, a bug in the App, or a problem on the resource that ran it. This page shows how to find failed jobs, read their logs, and run them again. ---

1. Open your project and select 3. Processing. 2. Summary lists failures under Failed, and automation problems under Needs Action. 3. For the full list, select Processes. Set the Status filter to failed, or search with the Process filter. ---

Select a process in the Processes table. The side panel opens: - At the top: the process name and these actions: - Quick add app: add another App to this process. - Quick add data: add datasets to this process. - Editor: open the process editor. - Delete: delete the process. - For each App in the process, three steps: Setup (its inputs), Run & logs and Results. ---

1. In the side panel, find the failed App and open Run & logs. 2. Under Logs, brainlife.io shows the error log from the resource (for example a slurm-.err file) when it finds one. If a summary of the failure is available, select Open logs or Open detailed log. 3. Turn on Advanced to browse all the job's files, for example: - slurm-.out: the full output from the resource. - config.json: the settings and input paths the App received. - Other files the App wrote before it failed. 4. Configs shows the configuration the job ran with; you can copy or download it as JSON. ---

What you see: the log reports a missing file or an unexpected format (for example FileNotFoundError: dwi.bvals not found). A process runs Apps one at a time, by hand. That suits trying an App on one subject. To run the same Apps on tens or hundreds of subjects, build a pipeline. A pipeline is the set of automations in a project. An automation runs an App for every subject and session that has the inputs and does not yet have the output. (Older pages call automations "rules".) ---

1. Each automation names an App, its settings, the inputs it needs (datatypes, tags, subject and session filters) and the outputs it archives. 2. brainlife.io checks each subject and session in the project. When a subject or session has all the inputs and lacks the output, the automation submits the App for it. 3. When the job finishes, the archived output is a dataset in the project, and it can be the input of the next automation. 4. If one subject fails, only that subject stops at that step. The rest continue. When you fix the problem and the missing output appears, the next automations pick that subject up. ---

A dataset is one item of project data: the files of one datatype for one subject (and session). For example: A neuro/dwi dataset holds dwi.nii.gz (the 4D diffusion image), dwi.bvecs and dwi.bvals. The FreeSurfer output for one subject is one dataset that holds all its surface and segmentation folders. The files of a dataset do not change after it is created. Its metadata (subject, session, description and annotations) can be edited. Older pages call a dataset a "data object"; that term is still used inside publication releases.

Apps exchange data through datatypes. A datatype defines the files and folders a dataset of that type contains. The colored chips on an App show which datatypes it takes as input and which it produces as output. Datatype tags (for example acpc_aligned or preprocessed) narrow a datatype, so an App receives exactly the input it needs. Browse all datatypes under Datatypes in the sidebar.
Annotations are free-text labels you add to datasets (for example control or patient) so you can filter them. ---

The sidebar has two parts. The top part (no heading) holds your own work: Dashboard: what needs your attention, your recent projects, your runs, and the compute you have used. My Projects: projects you administer, contribute to, or follow as a guest. My Publications: publications you authored, contributed to, or created. My Resources: compute resources you administer. My Apps: Apps you maintain. My Datatypes: datatypes you maintain. The Explore part holds what the community shares: SKAI: the AI assistant that answers questions about your projects, data and runs. Public Publications: all publications. Public Datasets: open data from DANDI, EMBER, BossDB, OpenNeuro and the brainlife.io Dataset Library. Apps: the App catalog. Datatypes: the datatype catalog. Public Projects: projects shared with the brainlife.io community. * Public Resources: shared compute resources. At the bottom of the sidebar are Login / Logout and the light and dark mode switch. ---

A project is your workspace: data, processing, notebooks and publications, shared with your team. 1. In the sidebar, select My Projects. 2. Select Project (the button with a plus sign). 3. In Create project, enter a Title and a Description. 4. Select Create project. brainlife.io creates the project and opens it.

Every project has five numbered tabs: 1. 1. Overview: the project's About text, Citations for the Apps and resources used, Related Articles, the people (Admins, Members, Guests), data agreements and resources. 2. 2. Data: the Project Data table of all datasets, with filters and actions. 3. 3. Processing: three views, Summary, Processes and Pipeline. 4. 4. Analysis: Jupyter notebooks that run against your project data. 5. 5. Publications: the publications made from this project. ---

Open the 2. Data tab and open the Project Data menu. It offers: "Copy Data from Public Datasets" (BossDB, DANDI, and OpenNeuro). "Copy Data From another Project": search for a project and copy its data over. "Upload Data From local Files": shown as "Currently unavailable". "Upload Data from ezBIDS": shown as "Currently unavailable". To bring in your own data today, convert it with ezBIDS on the web, or upload it with the brainlife.io CLI. aimport, a local importer, is new and not yet released.

1. In the sidebar, select Public Datasets. Search, or filter by source (Dataset Library, DANDI, EMBER, BossDB, OpenNeuro). 2. Select a dataset to open it. For a Dataset Library dataset, open its 2. Data tab to see its subjects, sessions and datatypes. 3. Use the Datatype filter to show only the datatypes you want (for example anat/t1w). 4. Select Copy to project. In Copy data to project: Under "1. Select the datatypes to copy over", tick the datatypes you need. Choose Existing and pick a project, or New project and enter Title (required) and Description (required). * Select Submit. The datasets appear on the project's 2. Data tab. ---

You can look at images, segmentations and tractography in your browser without downloading them. 1. On 2. Data, the table lists your datasets by subject and session, with their datatype, tags and annotations. 2. In a dataset's row, select Visualize (the eye icon) and choose one of the viewers registered for its datatype, for example NiiVue or Neuroglancer. 3. To overlay compatible datasets (for example a T1w image and a mask), select them and choose Visualize together. 4. Select a dataset to open it. Its Provenance (history) tab shows which App, configuration and inputs produced it. ---
You run Apps in two ways: a process, where you choose the data and Apps by hand, and a pipeline, where automations run an App for every subject and session.

section: Run an App in a process
content: 1. On 2. Data, select the datasets you want to process and select Stage to process. 2. In Add to process, choose "Create a new process" and give it a name, or "Add to an existing process". Select Add and open editor. 3. In the process editor, select Add App. Follow the steps Select App, Configure App Settings, Select Inputs and Configure Outputs. Choose whether to Archive Output (save the result as a dataset in the project), then select Add App. 4. Follow progress on 3. Processing → Processes. Select a process to open its side panel with Setup, Run & logs and Results. A job's status is shown as REQUESTED, RUNNING, FINISHED, FAILED, STOPPED or REMOVED. If a job fails, open its logs; see Troubleshooting.

1. Go to 3. Processing → Pipeline. 2. Select Automation (the button with a plus sign). Follow Select App, Configure App Settings, Configure Inputs and Configure Outputs (tick "Archive this output"), then select Complete. 3. Optional: select Automation Group to organize automations, and use Global Subject & session filters to limit which subjects and sessions run. The automation runs its App for every subject and session that has the inputs and does not yet have the output. Watch Summary for items under Needs Action. See Pipelines. ---

1. Open the 4. Analysis tab and select New analysis. 2. Choose a notebook from Blank Template Notebooks or Notebooks from Publications, then select Create. 3. Open the notebook from the Analyses list. When you are done, select Close and deactivate notebook, or Stop in the list. See Analysis with notebooks. ---

aimport is a new command-line tool (bl aimport) that imports neuroscience data (neurophysiology, neuroimaging and microscopy) from your own computer into a brainlife.io project. It works out what each series, image or recording is, converts it to BIDS, removes identifying information, validates the result and lets you look at it. Only then is anything uploaded. aimport is new. It is not in a published release yet, and it does not appear in the brainlife.io app. The steps below run it from development branches. See Status below. aimport is part of ezBIDS and reuses its mapping, conversion and defacing tools. ezBIDS on the web runs on a server; aimport runs on your computer, so raw data never leaves it. | | ezBIDS on the web | aimport (on your computer) | |---|---|---| | Neuroimaging | MRI, PET | MRI, PET | | Neurophysiology | MEG | EEG, MEG, iEEG, NIRS, EMG | | Microscopy | | OME-TIFF, CZI, ND2, LIF, SVS, PS-OCT, light-sheet (VISoR), OME-Zarr | bl aimport is in the brainlife.io Python command-line tool, pybrainlife (branch enh/cli); it is not in a published release yet. It runs the aimport engine, a Docker image (brainlife/aimport:dev) that is not published yet: build it from the ezBIDS repository. ezBIDS desktop with AI import (beta) is coming, Mac first.

Install bl (Python 3.8 or newer) and log in: Build the engine image from a clone of ezBIDS (Docker needed): Then import a folder into an existing project (--project is required): - --qa: after validation, open the output in the local QA viewer and ask before uploading. - --remote : add a remote microscopy source (https:// or s3:// OME-Zarr, NIfTI or TIFF), read by range requests, never downloaded whole. Repeatable. - --no-upload: stop after validation; nothing is sent. - --deface pydeface|quickshear, --target bids|datatypes, --work , --keys , --image , --tag , --yes: see the pybrainlife README or bl aimport --help. To try it first on public sample data, follow the aimport examples; they upload nothing. To let an AI model help name the series, set AIMPORT_MODEL and your provider's key (Claude, OpenAI, or Qwen through Ollama, which keeps everything local). Without a model, built-in heuristics do the work.

1. Scan the folder: what each series, image or recording is. 2. Review the plan: BIDS names, subject and session IDs, defacing, event names, metadata files. Every field can be edited. 3. Approve. Nothing is written before this; any later edit un-approves the plan. 4. Convert and de-identify: write BIDS, deface MRI, strip identifiers. 5. Validate with the BIDS validator (BIDS v1.11.2). Output with errors is never uploaded. 6. Look at the output in the QA viewer. 7. Upload to your brainlife.io project.

- The input folder (read only), original headers and file paths, the images before defacing. - The pseudonym key that links real identities to the new subject IDs. Keep it backed up; it lets a later import of the same person reuse their ID. - A remote or local OME-Zarr's chunk map. An AI model, if you set one, sees only a de-identified summary of each series, with every known identifier replaced by [x]. Never pixels, raw headers or paths.

DICOM or NIfTI. Identifying DICOM fields are dropped, names and IDs are redacted wherever they appear (descriptions, folder names, tables, README), dates are shifted by a fixed offset per subject (intervals kept), NIfTI header text is cleared, ages above 89 are written as 89. Anatomical images are defaced; only face voxels change. Screenshot and report series are excluded by default. ASL is excluded unless an aslcontext.tsv is supplied.

| Datatype | Accepted input | Written as | |---|---|---| | eeg | EDF/EDF+, BDF, GDF, BrainVision, EEGLAB, Neuroscan .cnt, Nihon Kohden, Persyst, FIF | BrainVision, EDF, BDF | | ieeg | the EEG formats, NWB | BrainVision, EDF (NWB input: NWB) | | emg | the EEG formats with EMG channels | EDF, BDF | | meg | FIF, CTF .ds, KIT, BTi/4D | FIF | | nirs | SNIRF, NIRx, Hitachi | SNIRF | Every recording is converted, never copied. Removed: patient and recording header fields, experimenter, device IDs; dates are shifted to before 1925 (scans.tsv keeps the per-subject shifted date); free-text annotations become event codes (E001, ...) that you name in review; channel names holding an identifier are renamed (eeg_007); head-shape points are dropped unless you keep them (fiducials and HPI coils stay). A final check re-reads every written file. Not converted (planned unsupported, with the reason): Artinis .oxy3/4/5 ("export to SNIRF first"), MEF3 ("export to EDF first"), EGI .mff, Blackrock, EEGLAB .set above 512 MB with embedded data, epoched or averaged FIF.

Read: OME-Zarr (NGFF 0.4 and 0.5), OME-TIFF, TIFF/BigTIFF (VISoR light-sheet stacks included), Aperio SVS, CZI, ND2, LIF, PS-OCT NIfTI and MATLAB .mat. Written as OME-Zarr. Not read (the plan says why): .vsi, .oib, .oif, .ims, .lsm, .scn, .mrxs ("export to OME-TIFF or OME-Zarr first"); raw PS-OCT .dat tiles ("reconstruct first"); unstitched tile mosaics ("stitch first"); PNG/JPEG; BIDS photo files. - Metadata rebuilt from an allowlist of image facts; the source's OME-XML, TIFF tags, slide labels and file names are never written. - Pixel size is never invented: it comes from the source; if it or its unit is missing, the plan waits for you to set it. - Labels and donors are pseudonymised: subject IDs come from the pseudonym key; sample and chunk labels are kept only when safe, else renumbered. - Reference datasets: an OME-Zarr input, local or remote, is read in place. aimport writes only new metadata; the chunks stay where they are and are streamed into brainlife.io on upload, one at a time.

section: Look before you upload: the QA viewer
content: Everything is served from your own computer (127.0.0.1), from the output only. - MRI: Neuroglancer, with each defaced image next to its original. The original shows the face: never screenshot or share it. - Microscopy: OME-Zarr in Neuroglancer; PS-OCT contrasts (reflectivity, retardance, optic axis) open as separate panels, never blended. - EEG, MEG, iEEG, NIRS, EMG: snapshots plus an interactive trace viewer (pan, zoom, event markers; NIRS as HbO/HbR). Bad channels. In the trace viewer, tick a channel bad, add a reason (flat, noisy, bridged, disconnected) and Save. aimport writes status and status_description into the recording's channels.tsv and validates again.

| BIDS | brainlife.io | |---|---| | MRI, PET | neuro/anat/t1w, neuro/dwi, neuro/func/task, neuro/fmap, ... | | microscopy | neuro/ome-zarr, one object per image, tagged with the technique (for example OCT) | | EEG, MEG | neuro/eeg/, neuro/meg/; channels.tsv (with bad channels) kept as the channels file | | iEEG, NIRS, EMG | project files with the BIDS tree (brainlife.io datatypes are drafts for now) | The mapping is one file, bidsbrainlifemap.yaml.

ezBIDS converts DICOM to BIDS in your web browser, with NiiVue built in. You do not need to install anything, program, use a terminal, or know the BIDS specification. BIDS (the Brain Imaging Data Structure) is a standard way to organize and describe neuroscience data. Data in BIDS is easier to share and can be processed by tools that read BIDS directly, such as BIDS apps. This page describes each step of converting data with ezBIDS. If you are new to ezBIDS, start with the ezBIDS tutorial.

The process of converting raw imaging data to BIDS is often time-consuming and can require substantial technical expertise. Furthermore, the BIDS specification, the rules governing how data must be described and organized, are complex and can be daunting for researchers relatively unfamiliar with BIDS. While there exist numerous tools for assisting users convert their data to BIDS (for complete lists, see here and here), these tools largely require technical expertise and knowledge of BIDS. ezBIDS was designed to alleviate these requirements. Specifically, ezBIDS provides unique features that differentiate it from other BIDS conversion tools: 1. No installation or programming required. It works in your web browser. 2. Semi-automated inference and guidance for BIDS adherence. It makes educated guesses about how your data should be mapped into BIDS and proposes both initial BIDS mapping of your data and warnings on the things that might need your attention. 3. Conversion of task event/timing files associated with functional BOLD (func/bold) sequences. If you have collected data using a task ezBIDS will help you map your tasks events into BIDS. 4. Multiple data management options: Download BIDS-converted data to a local computer or server. Send BIDS-converted data to open-science archives and platforms, such as OpenNeuro.org and brainlife.io. Think about ezBIDS as a small, smart, decision support system. ezBIDS attempts to do the heavy lifting for users, interpreting the necessa

Start by uploading your raw neuroimaging data to ezBIDS. Supported formats include DICOM and NIfTI. The platform will read your data and help you organize it according to the BIDS specification. Upon reaching the ezBIDS homepage, users can click on the "Get Started" button to begin converting their data. Users are then routed to the ezBIDS upload page, where imaging data will be uploaded to a secure server. Additional information regarding this upload process as it pertains to data access and control can be found here. Once uploaded, users are guided through several steps (i.e., web pages) to ensure that data are accurately described, organized, pseudonymized, and, ultimately, converted. These steps are described below: For ezBIDS to access users' imaging data, the data must first be uploaded to ezBIDS's secure and encrypted server (ezBIDS runs on a secure VM running on the HIPAA-aligned National Science Foundation's Jetstream-Cloud). There are two accepted upload methods: Raw DICOM data from the scanner or imaging device. NIfTI/JSON data converted from DICOMs using dcm2niix. If using this option, it is best if the most recent dcm2niix version was used. Data privacy Uploaded data can only be accessed through the unique URL with your session ID. Also, uploaded data are purged from the ezBIDS system after 5 days. ezBIDS prefers that non-anonymized data are uploaded (e.g. with the -ba y flag option in dcm2niix), as this makes it easier to discern the subject (and session, if app

This page allows users to provide general information regarding their dataset, such as authors, funding sources, etc. Users only need to provide information here the first time using ezBIDS with data from a new dataset. When using ezBIDS with newly acquired data from the same dataset as before, this information is already provided and is therefore redundant to specify again. Progress checks For this and subsequent ezBIDS web pages, certain information is required by BIDS, indicated on each page with a red asterisk or circle. These fields must be entered, otherwise, users will be unable to progress to the next page. This provides users with real-time assistance on what information is required in order to have BIDS-compliant data, rather than going through the entire process only to learn afterward that there is an issue to resolve.

On this page, ezBIDS provides the subject (and session, if applicable) IDs of the uploaded data. Users may edit or modify these fields as they see fit. This can either be done manually or by selecting an option within the "Reset Subject Mapping" button.

ezBIDS organizes all uploaded data into specific series and group IDs (grouping data). This is an intermediate step, that ezBIDS uses to facilitate editing entire series (or groups) of data files. Say, you want to change all the files from a single subject so that all the files start with a specific subject ID, or say you want to change all the data that are anatomical to start with the prefix anat, ezBIDS allows you to do that by grouping data for you by subjects, series, etc. Grouping procedure ezBIDS makes educated guesses about your data using information saved in the DICOM files. ezBIDS uses the DICOM fields Series Description, Image Type, Echo Time, and Repetition Time to group data together. This means that ezBIDS assumes that data with the matching values in these fields are part of the same series of data. ezBIDS then matches the Series to the corresponding BIDS entities. This grouping procedure saves users' time by serving files that might need to undergo similar changes in groups. ezBIDS provides warning messages (yellow circle and asterisk) to explain how the data were grouped. If this is incorrect and needs fixing, users can modify the groups using the graphical interface. If ezBIDS fails to group some of the data files, it will default to exclude the files, indicating that the files will not be converted to BIDS. Users may adjust this if necessary (or even mark data files not excluded by ezBIDS as 'to be excluded', e.g., localizer sequences). If a BIDS entity la

A critical feature of ezBIDS is the ability to support tasks and event files. If users collected functional BOLD (func/bold) data and have the corresponding timing files. The following are timing files formats compatible with ezBIDS: .csv, .tsv, .txt, .out, and .xlsx. A graphical interface guides the user in matching the files to BIDS structures. Importantly, ezBIDS comes with a beta feature and built-in compatibility with E-Prime files. When uploading timing files, it is crucial that the following entity labels be explicitly specified: subject, (session, if applicable), task, and run. These must match the corresponding func/bold sequences. This information can either be provided in the file path or as columns in the timing data themselves. Failure to do so will result in ezBIDS creating a placeholder value for any mismatched entity labels that will later require manual intervention. ezBIDS assists users in dealing with timing events and units BIDS requires that timing files be translated into events.tsv format, with several required and optional columns. Required columns include the onset and duration. ezBIDS has the ability to assist users in cases where uploaded timing files do not have a column that specifically pertains to onset and duration. For example, rather than a column specifying trial durations, a file might contain a column for trialonset and another column for trialoffset. Users can specify an arithmetic method (Subtract, Add) and choose the two columns that wh

Upon reaching this page, all individual imaging sequences are provided in the order they were collected for each subject’s (and session’s) scan. Here, users can make edits/modifications to individual files (e.g., set a sequence to exclude due to known participant motion, etc.) that were otherwise not possible when Grouping data. All modifications made on the Series Mapping and Events pages are applied. ezBIDS applies a run entity label to sequences if there were multiple occurrences during the scan. Functional data exclusion ezBIDS applies a volume threshold on 4D data (e.g., func/bold) to check for sequences that might have had to be restarted during the scan. The threshold is calculated based on the expected number of volumes collected during a 60-sec period, given the TR (60/TR). If a 4D sequence does not meet this threshold, ezBIDS sets the datatype/suffix pair to exclude, unless modified by the user.

Users have the option (recommended) to deface all anatomical images in order to further anonymize the data. ezBIDS provides two defacing procedures: Quickshear and pyDeface. Depending on the number of anatomical files in the uploaded data, this process may take several minutes, though ezBIDS can parallelize this process with concurrent defacing processes. If the defacing is suboptimal (i.e. defacing cuts into the brain itself), users may try again with the other defacing option or simply specify that they do not wish to deface the anatomical data.

For each subject ID specified, users may specify phenotypical information pertaining to each participant. By default, ezBIDS attempts to provide the sex and age of participants if this information is present in the metadata (typically only specified if non-anonymized data are uploaded). Users may add additional columns (e.g., handedness) or delete existing columns.

At this stage, users can click on the green "Finalize" button for ezBIDS to apply all user edits/modifications to create a BIDS-compliant dataset. Users may elect to keep any data that was set to “exclude” if they so choose. Once complete, two screens are presented. On the left is a Linux tree structure showing the BIDS dataset organization and file names. On the right is a screen output of the bids-validator, which provides a final check to ensure that the data are BIDS compliant. Any validator warnings appear in yellow and can be ignored (but it's good practice to resolve these at some point), and errors appear in red, indicating that the dataset is not BIDS-compliant for some specified reason and requires correction. If users need or wish to return to previous pages for additional edits/modifications they may do so. Then, upon returning to this page, users must click the green "Rerun Finalize Step" to apply all new changes. Once a BIDS-compliant dataset is generated, users can click on the blue "Download BIDS" button to download their zipped data to their local computer/server, and/or send their BIDS data to OpenNeuro.org or brainlife.io. In the brainlife.io app, the Project Data menu on a project's 2. Data tab lists "Upload Data from ezBIDS", but it currently shows "Currently unavailable". Start ezBIDS from brainlife.io/ezbids instead. Downloading non-BIDS compliant data Users may still download their BIDS dataset (or upload it elsewhere) even if the bids-validator return

ezBIDS provides additional features to assist users in converting their data to BIDS. 1. ezBIDS configuration templates ezBIDS creates templates for scanning sessions. Any scanning session processed using ezBIDS can become a template for future sessions. ezBIDS Templates can be reused to automatically load the BIDS mapping configuration a user has identified. Templates are helpful in the common situation where the same scanning protocol is used for multiple sessions. Often, researchers set up a scanning protocol and configure a series of scans to be acquired on multiple subjects across the duration of a research project. When the scans from the first subject are uploaded and processed via ezBIDS the researcher is effectively creating an ezBIDS Template, automatically. ezBIDS Templates are JSON files created every time a dataset is processed via ezBIDS. To use the template all the user has to do is download the template and upload the template with any new sessions acquired in the future. ezBIDS Templates can be reused for any number of datasets and reduce users' interaction with the ezBIDS graphical interface. More specifically, after ezBIDS has converted a dataset to BIDS, users have the option to download the file ezBIDStemplate.json. This file contains all information, to map the DICOMs to BIDS, including user edits and modifications, from the ezBIDS session. This file can be uploaded with new datasets. When done so, the information in the file is applied to the new ezBIDS

Although ezBIDS is a web-based service that does not require installation, it is possible to install it on your local machine or server. The main advantage here is that data is not uploaded to the ezBIDS server (i.e. data remains on-site). Instead, data is copied to one of the ezBIDS containers (brainlife_ezbids-handler) at /tmp/ezbids-workdir. However, with this approach users cannot upload their finalized BIDS-compliant data to brainlife.io via ezBIDS, as this requires authentication that isn't available with a local installation. Furthermore, setting up ezBIDS locally may require some technical know-how. The following steps should enable you to successfully install ezBIDS. Step 1: Software prerequisites Make sure the following software packages are installed on your computer: 1. Docker 2. Docker Compose 3. Node(.js) & npm Node and npm installation Download the LTS version (20.11.0), as ezBIDS does not work well with newer Node versions. To check that they are in your $PATH, enter "software --version" (e.g. docker --version) into your terminal. If successfully installed, a version ID will be displayed. ezBIDS is a community-driven project, and as such, contributions are both welcome and encouraged. For technical contributions, it is highly recommended that users locally install ezBIDS on their machine (see Installing ezBIDS locally section for details) and submit a PR for bug fixes and feature enhancements. For additional modality support requests (e.g., NIRS), users should reach out to the developers. A meeting and/or access to test data may be requested, as the developers are less familiar with imaging modalities outside of MRI and DWI.
